We use a series of models, ranging from simple to complex, to study how boundary conditions are affected by the cloud's properties. We hope this work will encourage the use of these models to better understand the early stages of supermassive black hole growth.

The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field near a stationary, perfectly conducting plane. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied on the boundary. This assessment considers how spontaneous emission rates change when an initially excited atom is accelerated versus an atom at rest encountering a moving mirror.

A longstanding issue regarding massive star origins involves whether these stars always form within dense clusters and, if found in less crowded environments, if they inevitably moved there.  Recent advances in wide-scale photometric surveys enable us to detect massive stars without bias in the less crowded regions of the galaxy.  This study examines forty candidate OB stars discovered by Mohr-Smith et al in the vicinity of Westerlund 2, with locations confined to a 1.5x1.5 degree square area, distinguished by their extinctions and K magnitudes.  Spectra from two extremely hot O stars show they are verified as O4V stars with masses exceeding 40 Msun.  Their velocity relative to Westerlund 2, measured against a binary-free reference point, is within specific km/s values.  Furthermore, with the aid of Gaia DR2 data on stellar motion, between eight and eleven O/WR stars might have been expelled from Westerlund 2 in the past million years, accounting for up to 25% of massive star expulsion efficiency, with their distribution showing near north-south alignment on the sky, implying a link between this outcome and sub-cluster unification coupled with the forces of dynamical expulsion.

Degraded handwritten documents, which are susceptible to damage from paper ageing and environmental factors, can cause severe readability issues for current text recognition algorithms. To overcome these challenges, we propose an innovative, end-to-end approach utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks that not only restores visual clarity but also improves the overall readability of the documents. This pioneering method differs from conventional binarization techniques, which primarily focus on enhancing visual quality, by integrating a text recognition module to optimize generated output. As a result, it exhibits improved performance on the H-DIBCO challenges, specifically in tasks involving Arabic and Urdu script recognition.

The growth of Information Technology has significantly altered how information is shared, making it necessary to convert printed text into digital format.  There has been an increase in fraudulent activities lately.  To prevent such account-related fraud, a system was devised which employs ID card extraction via OCR and NLP for verification purposes.  Optical Character Recognition, a technology that enables the conversion of images to text, can also be used to convert an Indonesian ID card or KTP into text format.  This facilitates easier data entry for service operators.  To enhance accuracy, service operators can then utilize Natural Language Processing to extract specific data from the text, such as full name, birth date, place of birth, etc.  This is particularly useful in preventing fraudulent activities by verifying user information before allowing access to their accounts.

In vehicular communications, the complex and dispersive nature of channels makes reliable channel estimation vital for optimal system performance, yet the IEEE 802.11p standard's limited pilots lead to inadequate channel tracking. As a result, conventional IEEE 802.11p estimators experience significant performance decline, particularly in high-speed scenarios. To overcome these challenges, researchers have explored deep learning (DL) techniques for channel estimation in IEEE 802.11p. Nonetheless, these approaches either underperform in extremely high-speed situations or exhibit substantial computational complexities. To resolve these issues, this paper introduces an innovative solution based on a long short-term memory (LSTM) model for channel estimation. The proposed method incorporates an LSTM unit for channel estimation, followed by a temporal averaging technique to mitigate noise, and analytically calculates the noise mitigation ratio to verify its effectiveness. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed solution surpasses the performance of recently proposed DL-based estimators, while also achieving substantial reductions in computational complexity.

The task of automatically assigning colors to images without human involvement has garnered interest within the machine learning community for a limited time. Colorization is particularly challenging due to its inherently high degrees of freedom; when presented with an image, multiple plausible color combinations exist, and there may be no single definitive solution. Another related issue is Single Image Super Resolution, a task that involves converting low-resolution images into higher-resolution versions. This research targets a novel, automatic colorization approach, specializing in astronomical images and leveraging Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). We experiment with employing various models in the RGB and L*a*b color spaces, relying on transfer learning and pre-trained ResNet-18 architecture, due to the small size of the dataset available. Our approach successfully produces aesthetically pleasing, high-resolution, and colorized results for images lacking these characteristics. The performance of the proposed model is quantitatively assessed by measuring distance metrics, including L1 distance and L2 distance, and evaluating the generated images against the real data distribution using the Frechet inception distance (FID) metric.

We've developed a novel numerical scheme to efficiently calculate Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) weights without relying on tedious iterative processes. Based on the Universal Approximation Theorem, our proposed method is characterized by a non-iterative equation, allowing for the direct computation of ANN weights. In addition to this primary approach, we present several modified schemes that balance computational efficiency with practical feasibility. All these schemes are thoroughly tested using a range of standard functional regression problems and a Monte-Carlo simulation design.

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's panel started representing the interests of young researchers within the ECFA community in January 2021. Throughout its first two years of operation, the panel developed its organizational framework, cooperated with ECFA by offering input and insights, and introduced several projects focused on comprehending and addressing the varied needs of young researchers. This report outlines the details of the panel's formation and operations as well as its engagement with numerous activities during its first two years of operation.

Confining modes at the edge, known as line waves, can propagate on the boundary between two specially designed electromagnetic interfaces that maintain mirror symmetry properties.
Studies have previously analyzed line waves in theory and in practice, revealing their occurrence at both microwave and terahertz frequencies.
It has been found that line waves exhibit unique characteristics, such as localized and non-localized modes, varying amplitudes on each interface, and discrete mode patterns.
A new type of optical device has been proposed, comprising a photonic crystal slab coupled with an optical wire, for amplifying line waves in the optical range.
The line waves' high confinement and single-mode operation make them suitable for supporting weakly dispersive and slow light systems.

One of the most effective approaches to building intelligent robotic systems is Learning from Demonstration (LfD), however research is still needed to overcome challenges such as multi-agent learning and long-lasting autonomy.  A new architecture for multi-agent LfD is introduced which enables the creation of reliable and efficient robotic systems in complex and large-scale environments by leveraging advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) through the implementation of a Federated Learning (FL)-based collaborative learning environment involving both humans and robots. This novel multi-agent LfD architecture is designed to overcome existing technological hurdles by integrating FL and True Distributed Learning (TDL) methodologies. It facilitates the creation of robust and adaptive robotic systems capable of navigating non-stationary environments by engaging both human and robotic agents in collaborative learning. This approach has far-reaching implications for future robotic development as it may shift the focus from traditional robotic structures to more decentralized and self-sustaining cognitive robotic architectures. Current research is evaluating the performance of this new architecture in various applications such as teleoperation and robotic learning, with promising preliminary results.

A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the mean absolute deviation of a median regression model, addressing the problem of irregularity that typically hinders conventional bias reduction.  To overcome this limitation, a specific alternative strategy was implemented.  Establishing the bias correction involves verifying the local asymptotic normality property and a specific Bahadur-Kiefer representation.  Developed within the context of a traditional asymptotic framework, this proposal appears to retain effectiveness in high-dimensional settings, as evidenced by simulation results.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of building a comprehensive knowledge graph. This connection has yet to
be fully utilized. In this paper, we bridge this gap by combining relation
extraction and knowledge graph link prediction into a single unified framework
known as relation discovery. This framework enables the identification of
knowledge graph links involving entities from diverse sets. Through extensive
experiments on datasets comprising both standard and domain-specific data,
along with the analysis of experimental findings, we showcase the effectiveness
of our proposed relation discovery approach. To achieve this, we developed a
custom-designed neural network that integrates entities, their attributes, and
the target relation through the application of multi-head attention.

The Analytical Exact Iteration Method has been employed to solve the N-dimensional Radial Schrödinger equation for complex-valued potentials, and further generalized to consider finite temperature and barychemical potential conditions in an anisotropic medium. By applying this approach, we calculated the bound-state energies of quarkonia, and found their behavior in the presence of anisotropy, temperature, chemical potential, and Debye mass within N-dimensional space. Interestingly, anisotropy was found to decrease the dissociation temperature of quarkonia, while chemical potential had a contrasting effect. Furthermore, calculations of the Debye mass were carried out for both vector and scalar gluons.

Our study focused on the magnetic arrangements within the crystals of Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7 using neutron-diffraction experiments. In Tb3RuO7, neighboring ruthenium atoms created a chain pattern, with some being ordered magnetically and others remaining randomly aligned. This unique combination resulted in an intermediate disordered state, with the two ruthenium types exhibiting similar yet distinct behaviors. In Nd3RuO7, the magnetic patterns were uniform and independent for the two ruthenium species, with both being ordered at temperatures below 17.5 K. Our findings indicate that the magnetic properties of the two ruthenium species in these compounds can be independently controlled through the chemical substitution of the rare-earth element.

Multi-Layer Perceptrons are particularly effective at generating accurate
low-dimensional representations of data, such as images, shapes and light
fields. Despite advancements using periodic activations or positional
encodings, they have historically been tailored to process a single signal
and sacrificed some degree of generality. We introduce an innovative new
approach to representation learning that not only generalizes well to multiple
signals, but outperforms the competition in fidelity. We utilize a unique
two-part neural network design, where a synthesis network produces the output
given a point in space (like a pixel's position) and a translation network
determines the input (like a pixel's texture). We also develop an innovative
training method that allows individual networks to be updated separately.
Consequently, our model exhibits the highest level of efficiency and is the
most flexible when processing multiple signals.

Traditional methods of covariate-shift adaptation utilize unlabelled data for either determining importance weights or domain-invariant features. Then, a model is trained using only labelled data. We're examining a special instance of covariate shift that also enables learning from unlabelled data, effectively merging adaptation with semi-supervised learning techniques. By drawing on causality concepts, we propose a novel method that requires learning from both the causes and effects of a target variable. This leads to the development of a semi-generative model, specifically a causal entropy-based model that generates causes and effects. Since the model is being trained to cover the entire causal structure, it can be viewed as a semi-supervised learning method with a built-in domain adaptation component. Experimental results demonstrate that this method performs better than conventional semi-supervised learning approaches and domain adaptation techniques.

Despite its impressive task execution capabilities, the inner workings of deep learning systems remain shrouded in theoretical uncertainty. In our study, we establish a geometric model for deep learning architectures by identifying connections to pre-existing geometric frameworks in quantum computation and diffeomorphic template matching. Within this context, we map the geometric structures of convolutional neural networks, residual networks, recursive neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and the equilibrium propagation framework. Furthermore, this geometric framework enables us to explore the relationships between geometric structures and the performance of different neural networks, thereby guiding the design of deep learning architectures at an algorithmic level.

We consider the field extension $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d},\zeta_3)/\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_3)$ where $\zeta_3$ is a primitive cube root of unity and $d$ is a positive cube-free integer. Our work examines the behavior of the chain of lattice minima in the cubic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d})$ arising from the prime factorization of $d$ in relation to generators of ambiguous principal ideals. Specifically, we investigate the occurrence of generators of such ideals among the lattice minima and explain their impact on the principal factorization type of the cubic field. Our results provide a detailed explanation of how certain generators of ambiguous principal ideals emerge from the lattice minima and contribute to a particular factorization type. We also establish how the field's factorization type can be derived from the chain of its lattice minima.

A research framework is introduced to uncover and analyze decision-making processes from deep neural network classifiers in jet substructure tagging techniques. To achieve this, the study uses a novel method, incorporating 'augmented' variables, known as XAUG variables, alongside standard input, then applies a layer-by-layer relevance analysis to both types of networks. XAUG variables are merged with intermediate network layers and utilised in final stages to interpret the classification outcome. Analysis shows XAUG variables enhance discrimination capabilities, and combining expertise from early layers with late layers results in accurate and interpretable tagging. This method is consistent with general feature selection methods and is applied to a jet mass discriminator in jet substructure applications, involving deep neural networks, where it identifies mass-related features in jet substructure images. This method is independent of network architecture and training algorithms and can be used across various deep neural network classifiers.

For every positive integer r, a specific kind of Stirling number is used to count how many ways a set can be divided into a specified number of non-empty subsets, where each subset contains at least r elements. We're introducing a variation of these Stirling numbers, which represents their extreme forms, reducing to well-known cases when r equals one. This paper seeks to establish formulas linking these variations together.

Eighty sets of layer groups were examined, each consisting of four layers, and 320 associated projection groups were determined. Additionally, the band parameters for each combination were calculated, leading to a total of 1,280 possible scenarios. Symbolic computations were successfully completed for all cases using the ATLAS computer algebra system. This work demonstrates the feasibility of symbolic computations for layer group properties, and new insights were gained, such as the layer group properties that occur within each of the 13 topological space groups found in the periodic table of standard tight binding models.

Momentum operators are explored in the context of intrinsically curved manifolds. It's established that for Killing vector fields representing these momentum operators, the manifolds are either flat or belong to specific categories: those with a compact structure and a constant sectional curvature of positive value, occurring in three or five dimensions. Counterexamples are also constructed to confirm that our findings are accurate.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem.

In a composite Higgs model, we explore the process of dark matter particle creation via hadron colliders. The complex scalar field, which develops a nonzero vacuum expectation to break the $SO(4)$ symmetry in the global $G/H=SO(4)/SO(3)$ symmetry, is responsible for the mass of dark matter particles. The lowest energy hadronic states, consisting of vector bosons, provide the interaction necessary for the creation of dark matter particles via a process known as "dark resonance scattering". Our proposal involves a composite dark scalar doublet, with one element developing a nonzero vacuum expectation after symmetry breaking, similar to the Weinberg cosmological model. The other element serves as a dark gauge boson with a mass generated by the "Higgs mechanism". The composite nature of the elements facilitates the creation of dark matter particles through multiplet production. Our model features a minimal particle content and can be differentiated through dark matter particle creation via various combinations of the elements. The process of dark matter particle creation via the "dark resonance scattering" of a $J/\psi$ meson offers an alternative to the standard $Z$ boson-mediated creation method.

The use of Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations, like redirected walking and haptics, extends VR interaction beyond conventional physical limitations by exploiting the boundaries of human perception, subtly guiding users' movements to enhance interactivity. This research examines the dangers of VPPM exploitation, beginning with a conceptual framework that confirms their existence and then applying it to haptic manipulation. By developing and testing a series of cunning strategies, we reveal that VPPMs can be exploited to undermine a user's perception of their location, causing them to unknowingly reveal sensitive spatial information. To protect against these threats, we propose a detection system that can identify and prevent potential VPPM exploitation, as well as offer users detection choices during interaction, essentially making VPPM utilization contingent on users' trust in the system.

To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into BigScience's large-scale, 1.3 billion parameter multilingual language model, initially trained on 13 languages. Our study focuses on key factors influencing model adaptability for new languages and weighs the computational expense against potential performance gains.

Recent high-resolution observations using VLA and CARMA telescopes have unveiled previously unknown details of proto-stars in binary systems. Specifically, it has been discovered that the total mass of the parent core significantly influences the mass of the binary fragments. Research indicates that massive binary stars originate from cores with low chemical composition. This finding has sparked interest in using binary star systems as indicators of star formation efficiency in the early stages of the galaxy's development. To further understand this process, it is essential to accurately simulate the formation of binary stars. In order to assess the validity of binary star formation models, it is necessary to compare them with data from observations of binary star systems. In this research, binary star formation is compared to observations of a system consisting of the stars CRA-EL 132298 and 132299. These stars are located near a molecular outflow and the observation of a binary star system through dust emission at a wavelength of 1.3 mm indicates that the system is young, suggesting that the star formation process is complete. Mass and velocity analysis of the system reveals that the more massive star has a mass of 15 solar masses while the less massive star has a mass of 9 solar masses. This research has determined that the system is at a distance of 230 parsecs, and based on the observation of the system's potential companion, it is estimated that the system formed from a core with a mass of 100 solar masses that had a angular momentum of 90 of its potential

This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach ('m-ar-K-FastICA') for feature extraction, combining kernel-based dimensionality reduction with ICA to overcome the limitations of previous methods. Although the kernel trick offers a powerful way to tackle non-linearity, its effectiveness can be undermined by suboptimal kernel functions, leading to minimal improvements. Our work brings together the beneficial properties of arcsinh and its robust kernel variant to enhance the separation of feature layers, thereby facilitating fast and efficient feature extraction. Furthermore, the method's kernel and learning parameters are easily interpretable, thus circumventing common pitfalls in machine learning. The proposed m-ar-K-FastICA approach surpasses state-of-the-art techniques in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency, as validated through extensive simulation studies and a real-world data application. The accompanying code is available for reproduction of results in https://github.com/joaoantunhes/marKFastICA.

This paper builds on existing research linking finite model theory to algebraic and propositional proof systems. It's proven that if a logic system can identify unique, non-isomorphic graphs in a specific category, then a related proof system can do so as well, at roughly the same computational cost. This allows researchers to apply existing bounds from the latter system to the former, shedding new light on CPT's limitations. Establishing a polynomial CPT lower bound via a related PTIME-instance could resolve a long-standing question in finite model theory. Additionally, the findings provide a theoretical explanation for the separation between polynomial calculus and extended polynomial calculus within bounded-degree settings.

A subring collection in a ring $R$, that is associative, commutative nor unital, is defined as proper subrings set-theoretic union equating $R$. If such a collection exists, the ring covering number $\sigma(R)$ in $R$ is determined by the cardinality of a minimal collection, and a ring is $\sigma$ elementary when $\sigma(R) < \sigma(R/I)$ for any ideal of $R$, given it is non-zero, two sided and in $R$. The given text describes the discovery of first ring $\sigma$ elementary instances which possess non-trivial Jacobson radical $J$  and a ring that is non commutative in $R/J$, while determining ring covering numbers in $R$.

Social media platforms host an immense volume of content, encompassing a broad array of views on society. Despite the numerous topics covered, identifying information to verify becomes arduous due to the sheer volume of posts. Even more challenging is ensuring the accuracy of facts across different languages, as each language hosts an extensive array of content. To tackle this issue, a system has been proposed to make facts more accessible. By analyzing tweets, the system extracts relevant information on claims and their associated evidence. Based on this data, a neural network is trained to predict the likelihood of each piece of evidence supporting a particular claim. Since verifying facts is subject to human bias, the system also aims to recognize instances of biased evidence. By incorporating a regularization technique that accounts for human preferences, the system is trained to distinguish between evidence related to humans and non-human entities. Experimental findings indicate that the system enhances accuracy when enforced and surpasses existing benchmarks in fact-checking. Moreover, the system is designed to be adaptable to various languages by incorporating a module that processes linguistic characteristics. Such an understanding of preferences enables the system to recognize challenging instances of fact-checking content.

Identifying trending social media events in real-time is crucial for applications such as tracking natural disasters, sports events, or political debates. Event detection is hindered by imprecise event definitions, resulting in low recall rates. To mitigate this, we introduce a new approach that leverages related events to improve recognition, utilizing a technique called "event family" propagation. Event similarity is assessed through keyword similarity and, in this study, PropEvent is compared with more standard event detection methods on public datasets. The results indicate that PropEvent surpasses other methods in terms of precision while maintaining competitive recall rates.

A novel method to analyze cosmic structures and parameters makes use of the weighted skew-spectrum by utilizing bispectrum statistics. This method incorporates skewness weights in addition to the traditional Gaussian likelihood, enabling more comprehensive assessment of non-Gaussian phenomena. Research indicates that, at the present stage of development, incorporating the weighted skew-spectrum does not substantially alter the estimated parameters. However, with enhancements and increased data, this method may offer a valuable supplementary technique in the upcoming decades.

By integrating Bayesian learning into adversarial training of deep neural networks, we developed a rigorous framework for training certifiable Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). This approach combines constraint relaxation and modified cross-entropy loss to achieve robustness to potential attacks. The method, demonstrated through empirical tests on standard datasets, allows for training BNNs that are both accurate and certifiably secure on challenging datasets such as MNIST and CIFAR-10, further providing benefits in uncertainty calibration. This innovation facilitates the deployment of BNNs in applications requiring utmost reliability.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicted the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that anxiety, uncertainty, and fear were crucial factors contributing to the spread of online rumors during public health crises, and that incorporating anxiety into predictive models yielded superior outcomes. Despite minimal reductions in the complexity of our models, our results showed considerable potential for applying machine learning to mitigate the spread of online rumors.

This study investigates the impact of hyperspectral pixel dimensionality reduction on classification tasks. Five methods (PCA, KPCA, ICA, AE, and DAE) are utilized to compress high-dimensional pixels down to 301 dimensions. The resulting pixels are used for classification, allowing a comprehensive assessment of each method's effectiveness based on classification accuracy, compression rates, and reconstruction errors. Our research employed three diverse hyperspectral image datasets (urban, suburban, and forest landscapes), gathered by the Remote Sensing and Spatial Ecosystem Modeling lab at the University of Toronto. Our analysis reveals that PCA, KPCA, and ICA methods preserve pixel signals well but show decreased classification performance beyond 90% compression rates. In contrast, AE and DAE achieve better results at 95% compression but see their performance deteriorate as the compression rate approaches 97%. Ultimately, our findings highlight the importance of considering both compression methods and rates when crafting an effective hyperspectral pixel classification workflow.

Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors but they pose significant challenges due to their large sizes. Understanding the underlying mechanisms of their successful formulations, such as the role of biases and widths of their layers, is essential for their optimal utilization. Previous research indicated that neural networks can identify valuable weights within untrained networks, which motivate the "lottery ticket" hypothesis. In this study, we analyze and demonstrate that neural networks' widths also bear inherent generalization capabilities. Our findings reveal that increasing the width of a neural network's earlier layers enhances its ability to represent diverse data, while also reducing overfitting tendencies. We confirmed this correlation through experiments on a range of standard image classification benchmarks. Our analysis suggests that increasing the width of a neural network's earlier layers enhances its ability to represent scene structure, which in turn facilitates generalization. Our widths-based generalization hypothesis complements the identified "lottery ticket" hypotheses, which relate to the network's sparsity and early stopping, respectively.

A novel prediction method, referred to as ProCS, enables fast and precise calculation of crucial chemical shift indicators in proteins. These indicators, associated with amide protons in proteins, are vital for assessing the proteins' three-dimensional structure. ProCS is grounded in a simplified empirical rule and can compute these indicators for any given protein structure in a matter of milliseconds. Compared to other methods, ProCS achieves the best balance of speed and accuracy, especially when applying it to structures determined through other methods such as X-ray, nuclear magnetic resonance, or computational modeling. ProCS is now available for public use at no cost via a web-based interface.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant.

Describing the behavior of complex systems comprised of strongly interacting elements requires concise expressions for their internal relationships. Ensuring the stability of these systems is possible if their internal components maintain a balance and coherence, which is the primary focus of parquet theory. This theory involves a set of nonlinear equations that govern the allowed interactions within the system. For systems governed by quantum mechanics, these interactions are restricted by symmetry rules. Previous work had established a set of rules for deriving allowed interactions, which was further developed to include a more general form of symmetry through a more precise mathematical structure, known as a braided tensor category. This more general form of symmetry allows for the derivation of more complex interactions, leading to a more comprehensive understanding of the system's potential dynamics. This more comprehensive understanding is represented by a more extensive parquet theory, which is shown to have a corresponding set of solutions that can be represented by a more extensive mathematical structure, known as a higher-category theoretical framework. This higher-category theoretical framework provides a more general and extensive mathematical structure for understanding the system's potential dynamics.

The process of exciton condensation leads to the spontaneous creation of electron-hole pairs and triggers a phase transition in a semimetal that forms an excitonic insulator by creating a gap at the Fermi surface. This theoretical concept has been around for decades, but current approaches only offer approximate solutions; therefore, a new method is required to study this phenomenon. By reevaluating the behavior of semimetals with the highest weight of their band structure at the Fermi point, an existing perturbation theory can be reformulated to systematically analyze exciton condensation while maintaining exactness. This reformulated perturbation theory allows for the accurate calculation of excitonic correlations and finds that exciton condensation occurs when a specific criterion related to the Fermi velocity is met, and as it nears a critical value, the gap diverges linearly. Furthermore, by integrating the concepts of emergent symmetry and fermionic mean field approaches, an exact effective Hamiltonian is derived, enabling the analysis of exciton condensation through a new parameter, related to the Fermi velocity, that controls the entire phase diagram.

In the US, various safety organizations have adopted text-based systems for processing community members' incident reports, which necessitated a closer look at the interactions between community members and dispatchers through these platforms. To investigate, researchers analyzed the system logs of LiveSafe, a community safety tool, combining quantitative and qualitative methods to identify patterns in the conversational flow. By developing a data framework that captured common incident-related information, researchers discovered dispatchers requested specific details from users, and emotional support from dispatchers increased the likelihood of receiving follow-up information, leading to improved response rates. Furthermore, two themes emerged from a close reading of 25 rich codes containing insightful comments from users: (1) users appreciated compassionate dispatchers, and (2) incident complexity was linked to the amount of information provided. These findings have been shared with the system administrators to foster collaboration and inform the design of similar community safety systems, with promising implications for enhanced human-computer interaction.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility. In particular, following the breakdown of the Fay-Dyson rule, the contribution of electron-electron interactions to magnetic susceptibility is found to be divided among intra-band and inter-band interactions, with the latter exhibiting an unusual sign change across a particular critical angle of momentum.

Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, representative samples to be annotated by a human. Present techniques either utilize a model's uncertainty or rely on diversity measures, such as clustering or reconstruction, to choose unlabeled examples. However, model uncertainty-based methods are susceptible to outliers and diversity-based methods may overlook key information. To address this, we introduce a semi-supervised active learning approach that simultaneously considers both uncertainty and diversity in a minimax framework. Our method incorporates a network that minimizes entropy and a discriminator that maximizes uncertainty, both optimized through adversarial training. As the algorithm progresses, it engages a human to label selected samples, effectively adapting to the available data. Experiments on image classification and semantic segmentation showcase our method's superior performance compared to state-of-the-art techniques.

To study how music changed over time from the year 1960 to 2010, we measured the
variety of songs in the Million Song Dataset using several elements, including
melodic quality, texture, volume, and rhythmic patterns. By analyzing the popular
hits listed on the Billboard Hot 100 and applying a statistical model, we found that
most songs became more predictable in terms of melody and simpler in composition
over the studied period. Although new technologies were expected to increase the
variety of music, our results show the opposite: that the use of computers and digital
recording equipment may have contributed to this outcome by making it easier to
produce uniform music.

A novel category of stochastic processes that incorporate reinforcement involves sequences of random groupings denoted as $\{\mathcal{P}_t\}_{t \ge 1}$. These process sequences, labeled as $\{\mathcal{P}_t\}_{t \ge 1}$, undergo modifications at discrete time intervals, with each modification governed by a probability distribution that is dynamic and adaptive. When the process is updated at time $t$, there are two possible outcomes: a new element either joins an existing grouping with some other items or creates a new grouping separate from any others. The decision behind adding to an existing grouping or starting a new one is controlled by a time-dependent probability parameter. Under specific conditions, it is demonstrated that these processes converge towards a specific equilibrium state. Specifically, it is proven that, under the condition that the decision-making probability tends towards $1/2$ as $t$ approaches infinity, the sequence of these processes converges towards a point where all groupings have the same size. A mathematical description of the convergence, denoted as $\mathcal{T}_\infty$, is expressed as the intersection of an infinite number of sets, each corresponding to a time point $t$. The convergence of these processes is, however, hindered by the use of time-dependent decision-making probabilities. The most extreme form of time-dependent decision-making involves starting new groupings only when they are initialized. Despite this limitation, it is proven that these processes still converge towards a common

Prawitz identified a key feature of Gentzen's intuitionistic natural deduction as the inversion principle, typically paired in proof-theoretic literature with the recovery principle. In contrast, this paper presents an alternative, by reformulating both principles into a single requirement, referred to as the harmony condition, within the context of the Computational Ludics framework. This new framework illuminates the underlying notions: that the inversion principle embodies containment, while the recovery principle serves as its converse. Additionally, this paper derives and demonstrates the equivalence of the harmony condition with two further conditions defined in the Computational Ludics framework.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks.

We show that a topological space's Smyth powerspace is core-compact if and only if the original space has local compactness. Consequently, this implies the Smyth powerspace does not uniformly preserve core-compact properties.

We're investigating singular vorticities in ideal two-dimensional fluids with specific properties derived from point vortices and vortex sheets. These characteristics are embodied in "pointed vortex loops," allowing us to concentrate on their corresponding orbits under area-preserving diffeomorphisms on the 2D real plane. The results show that a specific subgroup within these diffeomorphisms preserves the shape of the vortex loop itself, indicating the configuration space is comprised of loops confining a fixed area regardless of the vorticity distribution and any connected points.

The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is a causal parameter that can be estimated in two steps, initially modeling treatment and outcome to incorporate potential confounders, then applying predictions to ATE estimators, such as AIPW, with potential alternatives being Machine Learning algorithms due to their non-parametric nature and capability to handle complex relationships. In order to improve the efficiency of two NN models with no parameter regularization except SGD, our simulations indicate the significant drawbacks of AIPW when compared to its variant, nAIPW. The proposed estimator, a modified version of AIPW with NN, shares double robustness and causal consistency with nAIPW, and has the potential to be doubly robust, although this depends on specific model specifications. The introduction of l1 regularization in the first step of NN models has been found to significantly influence the performance of the AIPW estimator, while having negligible impact on nAIPW when employing l1-regularized NN models in the second step. In conclusion, under certain conditions, the proposed nAIPW estimator has been shown to be a more efficient method of estimating the ATE when employing NN models.

The role of $\tau$ is taking center stage in the current research into new physics triggered by lepton flavor universality violations observed in $B$-meson decays. Enhanced $\tau$ production at the Large Hadron Collider can be achieved by operating at higher luminosity with a tailored beam condition, known as the "High-Luminosity" or "HL-LHC" condition. This study examines the potential for triggering $\tau$-rich events at the upgraded HL-LHC conditions, focusing on the reconstruction of double tau leptons and studying the production of tau pairs in collisions involving protons and lead ions at energies of 2.30 TeV per nucleon pair. It presents the results of the trigger development for the CMS detector's 2015 architecture, demonstrating the feasibility of triggering on these events with a focused suppression of irrelevant background by designing an innovative, tau-specific trigger algorithm. This new approach results in a notable improvement in acceptance, allowing for a considerable increase in the acceptance of relevant processes over a wide range of background levels. This acceptance can cover up to $90\%$ with a background suppression of two orders of magnitude, with the potential to be even higher at higher background levels.

A tabletop-sized rotating annulus setup has been extensively studied to mimic the general circulation of mid-latitude atmospheric circulation. The device effectively replicates two crucial factors contributing to cyclogenesis, namely the influence of rotation and temperature variations, in a simple yet comprehensive arrangement. The laboratory model enables researchers to control and analyze the formation of baroclinic waves through adjustments in temperature gradients and rotational rates, thereby creating distinctive wave patterns at the free surface of the rotating liquid. These experiments were conducted alongside numerical simulations by five groups from the MetStr\"om collaboration, utilizing different methods and approaches to validate their results. The obtained wave patterns were then analyzed, compared, and documented to establish benchmarks that can be used to evaluate the performance of atmospheric numerical models in the future.

A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel approach to estimating the parameters of the Poisson process in a Bayesian framework, by transforming them using a tuning parameter'm'. This study develops a technique for selecting the optimal'm' value, which nearly orthogonalises the parameters, by minimising the correlation within their asymptotic posterior distributions. By choosing this optimal'm', the parameters converge faster and efficient sampling is possible using Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. Finally, parameter values are then extracted through a straightforward transformation. We present results from simulations involving models of both identical and non-identical extreme rainfall in Cumbria, UK.

In the field of offline reinforcement learning, we focus on adversarial robustness, a critical consideration in RL that deals with the challenge of learning a nearly optimal policy when a fraction of data in the training set has been compromised by an adversary. Our study begins by examining a worst-case scenario involving the linear Markov decision process and finding that even with the adversary only modifying the reward in each data tuple, a certain threshold of optimality gap cannot be avoided. Conversely, we identify a robust offline learning algorithm that allows for achieving a significantly better optimality gap than what is allowed by the martingale reward structure, all while relying solely on the knowledge of transition probabilities. The computational efficiency of our method is also examined and we show that it operates in linear time. Additionally, we expand our findings to soft Q-learning and establish the connection between its robustness and the known optimality gap results in the standard setting. Lastly, we move to the online setting and use the notion of Kalman filter to deal with the adversarial reward in MDP, achieving an $\sqrt{T}$ learning gap in the linear MDP and providing the first $o(\sqrt{\log T})$ learning gap in the finite MDP, with our analysis also accounting for the impact of initial conditions and epoch-length.

This study demonstrates a logarithmic convexity linked to observability at a specific point in time for a one-dimensional heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions, leading to impulse approximate controllability in similar scenarios with dynamic boundaries. Additionally, we provide a detailed estimate for the cost of impulse control. Our research includes a step-by-step procedure for finding the impulsive control of minimal L^2-norm and supports these findings with numerical tests to verify the efficiency of the developed algorithm.

A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We identified distinct behaviors of two major detection methods - model calibration and density estimation - in response to background and semantic shifts in data, which were found across various language understanding datasets. In our evaluation, density estimation outperformed model calibration in background shift scenarios but struggled with semantic shifts, with both approaches underperforming when confronted with unseen topics in low-data settings. As a result, we propose that density estimation and model calibration be considered as means to detect changes in foreground and background aspects of shifting distributions, respectively.

In recent years, various artificial molecular motors utilizing electric currents have been explored, and like Brownian machines, they generate directional rotation from random tunneling events. Despite their potential to drive molecular machines of the future, their theoretical modeling is understudied. Here, we create a mathematical model for simulating these systems and verify its validity by applying it to a simple motor driven by an electric field, and comparing its results to real-world experiments. By using the motor's microscopic structure, we were able to accurately model the current-flow dynamics that influence its rotational velocity and direction. This study sheds new light on the motor's motor dynamics by integrating its electrochemical behavior into the study of molecular dynamics.

Building on a 2014 framework, researchers introduced various interpretations of transducer behavior, some of which lacked clear determinability criteria. A new classification of transducers was established to address this. This study extends that work by integrating (1) transducers with their underlying transition graphs rewritten as graph rewriting systems, and (2) analyzing these systems under different acceptance conditions. Notably, we find that graph rewriting systems yield the same decidability outcomes as original semantics, whereas classical semantics produces contradictory results in certain instances. This study further explores special cases, including a particular type of two-way transducer, demonstrating improved decidability criteria in these instances.

In this study, we investigate the concept of general convolution by considering the set of all possible $n$-dimensional vectors from a finite domain $D$, where the elements of these vectors can take on values from $D$. A specific operation, denoted as $\oplus_f$, is defined as the element-wise sum of the components, modulo $f$ for each element. This enables us to define a new type of convolution, known as the $f$-Convolution, for two functions $f_1$ and $f_2$, where each function can be represented as a sum of products of vectors from the domain $D$. By applying $\oplus_f$ to these functions, the $f$-Convolution corresponds to a specific count, specifically the number of ordered $n$-tuples from the domain $D$ that result from the $\oplus_f$ operation. A brute-force approach would yield an $O(|D|^{2n+1})$ time complexity for computing the $f$-Convolution. In our case, we demonstrate that computing the $f$-Convolution can be achieved in $O(n \cdot 2^{n}\cdot \log^2 D)$ time, where $D$ represents the size of the domain $f$, and we subsequently present an algorithm capable of computing an approximation in $O(n \cdot 2^{n})$ time. Additionally, we analyze a more complex problem known as

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 offered initial insight into its composition, yet a detailed analysis with current spectroscopic methods has been lacking, especially concerning its atmospheric features, which display unusual properties and contradict earlier estimates of the dwarf's mass and orbit, fueling speculation to potentially siphon matter from its host star. We employed the THANOS atmospheric solver and the THAMES spectro-pyramid model to analyze a sample of high-quality spectra, taken between 0.815 and 4.2 microns, which we also fit using a Bayesian approach, considering variously aligned spectra, temperature and metallicity variations, and incorporating a systematic bias towards cooler temperatures, observed in the dwarf's atmospheric features. Our analysis supports earlier claims of the peculiar alignment of GJ 229B's orbit, which appears to be tilted at approximately 115 degrees, yet contradicts earlier estimates of the dwarf's mass, which we estimate to be around 23 to 35 junctions, equivalent to 20 to 32 times the mass of our Earth. We modelled the dwarf's atmosphere as cloud-free, featuring log(g) around 3.57, with temperatures ranging from 600 to 425 K in its upper atmosphere, and comprising the combination of photospheric features and water absorption bands that give the dwarf its distinctive red features.

To search for the potential existence of unique $0^{--}$ states, we created a systematic approach to designing tetraquark operators. In the process, we found that $[su]_{j=1}[nd]_{j=1}$, with both $SU(3)$ doublets in the same parity, can form a $0^{--}$ tetraquark operator. Subsequently, we computed corrections to its spectroscopic energy using QCD sum rules. Our results for the spectral density, and the resulting masses, suggest that $0^{--}$ states may not exist below 2 GeV. Although our approach is paradigmatic, our findings may provide valuable insights for experimental researchers.

A crucial goal of the LHCb experiment is to establish the $C\!P$-violating phase $\phi_{s}$ and decay width difference $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ caused by $\bar{b}\to\bar{c}c\bar{s}$ decays. The precise prediction of $\phi_{s}$ and $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ is crucial for understanding the mechanism of $\bar{b}\to\bar{c}c\bar{s}$ decays. We calculated the hadronic contributions to $\phi_{s}$ and $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ using the sum rules approach. The results indicate that the hadronic contributions to $\phi_{s}$ and $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ are essentially negligible.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is complex due to the interplay of turbulent airflow, gravitational settling, and infectious organisms' ability to survive for extended periods. To evaluate the effectiveness of particle filtration in bus ventilation systems, we're analyzing the combination of these factors. In order to simulate aerosol transport, we divided the bus into distinct zones using numerical methods and confirmed the accuracy of our approach by replicating and validating several key scenarios. Subsequent simulations examined the phenomenon of coherent flow structures, which significantly impact aerosol behavior and our understanding of airflow within the bus. By studying the residence times of aerosols, we're able to determine which zones of the bus are most susceptible to airborne pathogens. This knowledge, combined with the temperature distribution, will enable us to assess the efficacy of particle filtration in different sections of the bus.

This study has conducted large-scale shell-model computations for $\beta$-decay attributes. Researchers at ILL, Grenoble, recently performed $\beta$-delayed $\gamma$-ray spectroscopy to investigate $\beta$-decay properties related to the transition of $^{137}$Te ($7/2^-$) to $^{137}$I with various final $J$-values. We conducted a comprehensive shell-model analysis of nuclear properties and compared our results to experimental findings. We then reported our computed $\beta$-decay attributes, such as the $\log ft$ values and the mean shape factors. Our study marks the first theoretical calculation for $\log ft$ values in conjunction with these novel experimental data. We then generated a comparison between our computed $\log ft$ values and the observed results. The purpose of this study is to evaluate the reliability of shell-model calculations in understanding nuclear transitions and to facilitate the development of accurate nuclear input for practical applications in $\beta$-decay analysis.

Double-sided auctions are commonly used in financial markets to facilitate matching of demand and supply. Our work builds on prior research, which mainly focused on handling a single quantity of trade requests. To expand this knowledge, we developed methods to support multiple quantity trade requests and established fully formalized matching algorithms for double-sided auctions. These algorithms come with rigorous correctness proofs. Additionally, we formulated new theorems for verifying the uniqueness of an exchange's output, allowing for automatic detection of potential program violations. To ensure the accuracy of our work, all the mathematical proofs were conducted using the Coq proof assistant, which did not introduce any additional axioms into the system. From these formal proofs, we were able to derive verified and executable OCaml and Haskell code. To validate the practical value of our research, we successfully tested the verified code using actual market data from an exchange to simulate trade requests.

We utilized heavy quark effective theory to investigate the $F$-wave bottom mesons, applying both theoretical and experimental data to calculate the mass of these mesons. Additionally, by examining the decay widths of bottom mesons, we derived upper limits on their corresponding coupling values. Our research further included constructing Regge trajectories in the planes of angular momentum (J) and squared mass (M^2), yielding predictions that align neatly with Regge theory lines. These outcomes may hold significant implications for future experimental research on this topic.

Michal Szabados initially proposed a theory in his doctoral dissertation. In this current paper, the proposed conjecture is examined by the authors, specifically a Ph.D. hypothesis by Michal Szabados. Initially, the researchers demonstrate that an evaluation could be narrowed down to a periodic structure, defined over a specific and limited character set. It is further established that Szabados's conjecture is true for a considerable class of non-regular patterns. This includes all low-convex patterns of relatively simple complexity.

Dynamical systems that are informed by data are becoming increasingly common in a variety of fields, including high-energy physics, weather forecasting, and traffic analysis. They, however, pose a significant challenge to modeling and simulation due to three main issues. Firstly, such systems often lack a clear understanding of the underlying physical laws governing their behavior. Secondly, the data generated by these systems is inherently noisy. Finally, the non-linear relationships present in these systems complicate the process of pinning down their state. In this study, we present a novel approach that leverages quantum algorithms to develop a partial recovery of the dynamics of an unknown non-markovian dynamical system with a linear measurement constraint for each time step. We apply and experimentally validate this algorithm within a quantum simulator for low-dimensional systems, and we observe that the algorithm exhibits exponential scaling for higher dimensional systems, albeit with a preliminary, basic implementation.

The timeless appeal of chess persists, with its strategic intricacies still captivating players across the globe. As a result, the number of players is steadily increasing, with the FIDE listing more players each year. To help these players improve their game, our research involves creating a social network of chess players based on their skills. Meanwhile, an independent study mapped the connections between chess openings, presenting them as a clustered graph where related moves are grouped together. Such a relatedness network of chess openings can aid players in developing their opening strategies by suggesting similar moves when they encounter an unfamiliar one. To achieve this, we constructed a social network of chess players using the publicly available chess API, transferred the chess openings to a knowledge graph, and applied a knowledge graph embedding method to analyze the chess openings. Then, we used the embedded information to create a relatedness network of chess openings. Our results show that this relatedness network of chess openings allows for an efficient exploration of the chess ontology, while our analysis reveals an interesting link between the chess moves and their names. Additionally, we demonstrated the chess embeddings' ability to recommend similar chess openings based on a given move. Finally, we set up a case study to investigate the value of chess pieces, concluding that controlling the piece with the lowest value generally leads to a win.

This research explores the observational characteristics of millisecond pulsars in terms of their magnetic fields, rotational periods, and masses. Our analysis is grounded in the concept of accretion-induced collapse of white dwarfs within binary star systems, enabling a more nuanced comprehension of millisecond pulsar demographics.

A method to derive constants of motion outside local framework is applied to a class of dissipative mechanical systems.  For a class of Lagrangians with symmetry under smooth reparameterizations, first-order Hamiltonian formulations are developed.  The resulting Hamiltonian systems are shown to possess nonlocal constants of motion.  Crucially, these constants remain useful for solutions to partial differential equations representing the dynamic equations, providing key existence and estimate results.  The approach is illustrated by applying the method to a class of dissipative Lagrangies dependent on time and velocity.

Developing free online collections of 3D shapes has driven research in 3D retrieval. Debates surrounding the optimal input method for retrieval and the ultimate application have been ongoing. In this research, we present a practical solution by exploring an innovative way to collect 3D models through air-drawn gestures in virtual reality (VR) environments. We developed an approach to extract 3D shapes from users' sketch-like inputs using a novel technique of joint prediction. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, and user evaluations confirm its practicality. We successfully demonstrated the first air-drawn 3D retrieval system in a fully immersive VR setting, enabling users to find 3D shapes by freely drawing in mid-air.

HD80606b, a planet that passes directly in front of its host star, undergoes a significant 1000-fold increase in the heat it receives due to its highly eccentric 111-day orbit. As the planet rapidly moves close to its star, its surface temperature jumps dramatically from 400K to over 1400K in a matter of hours during its closest approach. Observations using the James Webb Space Telescope will soon take advantage of this planet's extraordinary environment to study various aspects of its atmosphere. Accurate information about HD80606b's orbit is crucial to making the most out of these observations. Researchers have conducted in-depth analyses of the planet's transits on February 7, 2020, and December 7-8, 2021, in collaboration with the TESS spacecraft. In addition to confirming what they already knew about the planet's highly eccentric orbit, their findings surprisingly indicated the presence of an unusual and irregular variation in the planet's orbital path, amounting to about 0.0006 of an arc second. Further studies are needed to confirm this discovery, as well as its potential connection to irregular variations in the planet's closest approach point.

In this investigation, we're looking at how a specific type of matter collapse, governed by a certain relationship between pressure and density, behaves according to the general theory of relativity. The effect of this relationship on the mass function is analyzed in terms of its consistency with the general relativity equations, and we find that when this relationship holds, it's usually difficult to get consistent solutions. The outcomes of this type of collapse are then explored, along with the effect of additional factors, such as pressure in a collapsing cloud. Since accurately modeling such a situation is hard due to lack of information about its dynamics, we consider small changes in density instead. These small changes cause tiny pressures and allow us to analyze the behavior numerically. Our study reveals that when there is no restriction on the pressure-density relationship, the resulting equations do not present incompatibility issues, in contrast to the situation where such a restriction is imposed.

Using the Iyer-Wald formalism, we have developed a comprehensive method for determining corrections to the extremality bounds and entropy of Kerr-Newman black holes following any arbitrary perturbation. This method involves integrating an effective stress tensor and shows, under certain conditions, the correction is equivalent to the standard stress tensor, thereby illuminating the relationship between extremality corrections and energy conditions. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that to lower the mass of an extremal black hole in a canonical ensemble as stipulated by the weak gravity conjecture, the perturbation must breach the dominant energy condition. We have successfully applied this method to compute higher-order corrections to black holes in anti-de Sitter space and to Kerr black holes.

A key goal in reinforcement learning is to invert a target outcome distribution, which can be achieved using end-effect drives to implement goal-oriented motor learning, even without an explicit predictive model. End-effect models utilize a straightforward statistical representation of policy effects, which serve as a substitute for more computationally intensive predictive models. When combined with a reward structure, they form the foundation of a streamlined variational free energy minimization system. However, the primary challenge is balancing the balance between exploring novel actions to expand the policy's effect space and refining existing skills. Which approach is optimal depends on the specific scenario, particularly the size of the target distribution and the policy's current effect coverage. Despite existing research on this topic being limited, we thoroughly investigated the exploration vs. exploitation tradeoff and its consequences for diverse end-effect drives. Moreover, we introduced an efficient merit drive that surpasses traditional random and axial explorations in reward optimization.Merit drive experimentation results reveal its superiority over these alternatives, along with its resilience to disruptions in scenario dynamics without compromising its performance.

A generalized three-dimensional Poincaré algebra has been developed that incorporates colour symmetry. This enhanced algebra can serve as a basis for modelling coloured Poincaré gravity and exploring generalised models of massive and massless free particles in three dimensions. Multiple generalised particle models have been presented, which distinguish themselves in terms of the coloured Poincaré orbits they describe. Our methodology provides a potential pathway to describing particles in non-abelian backgrounds and serves as a starting point for the worldline formulation of an associated quantum field theory.

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs.

Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.
Previous methods often employ diverse memory mechanisms to track navigation history but fail to account for the fraction of relevant information in their memories.
We propose the MemoNav, a novel memory-based navigation framework, designed to improve performance in multi-goal scenarios by selectively retaining both short-term and long-term memories in proportion to their relevance.
The MemoNav system consists of two primary components: a short-term memo keeper that uses attention-based recurrent networks to retain and update partial navigation history, and a long-term database that stores a transformed history in an external memory.
We employ episodic training to facilitate interaction between the short-term keeper and the long-term database, enabling the sharing of information and the learning of relevant memories.
As a result, the MemoNav system is capable of learning a memo strategy that is adaptive to the fraction of useful information in both short-term and long-term navigation history.
Our experiments on a new image-based goal navigation dataset demonstrate that MemoNav outperforms state-of-the-art models, and we further investigate the impact of various training protocols on performance.

To increase cellular capacity, operators initially implemented 4G LTE small cells by augmenting existing licensed spectrum, with later introduction of Spectrum Sharing via LTE-LTE Unlicensed (L-U) and LTE-V (5G NR non-standalone mode), with unlicensed and licensed spectrum being used in conjunction. However, with the advent of low-power, short-range technologies such as NB-IoT, NR-URLLC, and NR-UL, which require less licensed spectrum than traditional cellular networks, the spectrum shortage concern is minimized. Instead, the main issue becomes whether licensed spectrum is sufficient to support demanding applications, rather than just those with low demands. Consequently, the need has arisen for licensed and unlicensed spectrum to be used in conjunction, with the licensed spectrum being used as a backhaul for unlicensed small cells or low-power nodes. To address this use case, L-U and V have built-in features to support such an implementation, whereas NB-LL, NR-URLLC, and NR-UL, being low-power, short-range technologies, are not suitable for backhauling. As a result, the question arises as to whether L-U and V can support such an implementation, with the answer being yes, but with the implementation being overly complex and inefficient. Therefore, the focus has shifted to designing a more simplified and efficient implementation, with the goal of achieving higher throughput, with the numerical results demonstrating that the proposed implementation can achieve a 100% increase in throughput in scenarios with equal

We've developed a comprehensive framework to model complex interactions between multiple entangled systems using hypergraphs. This approach can be applied to several processes and we'll specifically explore how certain conditions lead to spontaneous pattern emergence in systems where individual units interact with each other. Our focus will be on two specific settings: one involving interactions between groups over long distances, and another with diffusive interactions between units. Additionally, we'll demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through applications to both the generalized Volterra system and the Brusselator model.

This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a continuous setting, thereby providing a connection to established methods for sparse operator growth that involve the quantum tensor network paradigm. Our work ultimately facilitates a comparison of operator growth behaviors in Lie-symmetric systems with those exhibiting sparse patterns.

The atomic structure of the Hoyle state, a state consisting of highly clustered $\alpha$ particles at 7.65 MeV in $^{12}\mathrm{C}$, has been a topic of interest for a long time. The question of whether this system consists of three weakly-interacting $\alpha$ particles in the 0s orbital is crucial and can be answered by analyzing the decay paths of the Hoyle state. The paper provides information about the breakup process of the Hoyle state by employing a novel experimental technique. The investigation of the direct decay channel of the Hoyle state into the ground state of $^{8}$Be has allowed for a more accurate analysis of the branching ratios of its decay pathways. The relative strength of the decay channels that release excess energy from the breakup of the Hoyle state was compared with Monte Carlo simulations of the nuclear structure, assuming that this structure consists of three $\alpha$ particles in the 0s orbital. The comparison of experimental and calculated decay ratios revealed that the 20 MeV continuum contribution to the $^{8}$Be yield has a weight of approximately 42\%. The study concludes with an interpretation that supports the concept of the Hoyle state as an $\alpha$-condensate, with a significant amount of its structure consisting of three interacting $\alpha$ particles in the 0s orbital.

Significant breakthroughs in understanding and/composite material fracture robustness come from studying fracture dynamics.  In two-dimensional brittle materials, where fracture dynamics behave analytically, the problem of cracking oscillations has been thoroughly researched for its practical implications on propagating cracks.  A new theoretical framework has been developed to explain the oscillations of cracks in three-dimensional materials through direct analysis of stress concentrations at crack edges.  The theory accurately predicts existing results for two-dimensional materials and extends the study to nonlinear crack propagation in two dimensions, adding a new perspective to the field.  The framework's capabilities are showcased through various numerical examples that highlight its potential applications and possible future research directions.

In a general setting, we examine the long-term performance of a class of information processing tasks known as $\ell$-error-disjointness problems over finite-state channels with feedback. This group of problems encompasses, among others, source coding with steganography and channel coding with feedback under constraints. It's proven that the optimal long-term performance for these tasks can be determined by a specific infinite-horizon single-user strategy. This finding leads to a novel characterization of the channel capacity with feedback for finite-state channels and a generalization of the Steiner formula. Additionally, it's shown that any sublinear lower bound on the long-term performance of $\ell$-error-disjointness problems over channels with feedback applies universally to all such problems, including those with unique optimal solutions. This result contrasts favorably with the case of non-finite state channels. This research further develops a new strategy for achieving optimal long-term performance on specific tasks, such as source coding with steganography, and provides a new characterization of the channel capacity with feedback for a significant class of finite-state channels, including erasure channels and a significant segment of deterministic channels.

A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may be used to create fault-tolerant quantum computations via topologically non-Abelian states. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair-breaking when present. Additionally, we found that Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance caused by the Zeeman field through mixing, thus restoring superconductivity. Furthermore, we established that Rashba coupling's favorable impact on superconductivity originates from a spin-flip driven enhancement of the likelihood of a pair of electrons traveling in reverse time-states. Our analysis also predicts that Rashba coupling could be feasible in the experimentally accessible parameter range necessary for non-Abelian topological processing.

This study focuses on understanding and interpreting tables, requiring the ability to recognize their structure, compare data, and make generalizations. To achieve this goal, we introduce a new dataset for SemEval 2020 Task 9: Analyzing Interpretations of Tables, with a dual objective of identifying and evaluating factual claims related to tabular data. The task comprises two sub-tasks: firstly, to verify all the factual information presented in a table, and secondly, to extract and summarize the top-level conclusions drawn from this data. In addition to specifying evaluation criteria, we provided training and testing tables for both sub-tasks, requiring participants to submit their analysis and interpretations of the provided tables. The detailed results and feedback from participants can be found in the workshop paper submitted to the SemEval-2020 proceedings.
