Our proposed algorithm, Feature Mapping RNN, leverages key concepts in machine
learning, including parameter sharing, Radial Basis Function kernels, and
adversarial training, to develop a novel RNN architecture for generating future
video features and anticipating actions. By using only the initial video frames and
a reduced number of parameters, Feature Mapping RNN efficiently generates future
features, which are then used in a multi-layer perceptron to forecast actions.
When evaluated on the challenging ActivityPension dataset, our method exhibited
spectrum-agnostic performance, surpassing top existing approaches while exhibiting
adversarial resistance on various activity datasets, such as HuRePe and OKN. Our
method also exhibited the fastest processing speed, particularly in a study on
adversarial resistance where our method demonstrated a significant 87% reduction
in processing time compared to the second-best approach.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which have significantly expanded our understanding of these events and their implications. Studies of these flares have taken several key aspects into consideration when evaluating their potential as exoplanetary biosignatures and assessing the planetary habitability. These factors include the rarity of large flares, the duration of time available to search for signs of atmospheric changes, and the atmospheric recovery time following these events. Analysis of these factors indicates that small planets such as those represented by the TESS small planet population may be well-suited to support life due to their proximity to their host stars, as long as their host stars do not exhibit the most extreme behavior. This is because even moderate-sized flares observed by these missions emit enormous amounts of energy, confirming that low-to-moderate energy flares can trigger atmospheric changes on small planets. Ultimately, future missions such as the TESS and PLATO missions are well-positioned to make several breakthroughs in our understanding of these factors, which in turn will inform efforts to find life beyond our solar system.

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to define the deformation space of the canonical connection on nearly G2-manifolds with a normal homogeneous structure of four dimensions.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a specific condition with respect to a closed subspace $C$. This condition is: there exists a closed subspace $M$ such that $TM \perp M^\perp$ and $TC = MT^*. $ We provide examples and demonstrate that certain operator classes, including C-wyld and C-pseudo Hermitian, are subsets of C-normal operators. Additionally, we establish a key inequality for C-normal operators.

This paper delves into a type of partition that excludes elements divisible by $p$, specifically examining those with no elements divisible by $p$ themselves. To address congruence issues related to these partitions, a method using 'letters' is developed, where the mod $p$ behavior of a partition is determined by a subset of its components. Using this framework, existing results on $p$-core $p'$-partitions can be reevaluated through a modified generating function approach. As initially observed, this method facilitates the determination of counts modulo $p$, even when a general enumeration is challenging. In cases where $p$ equals $5$, an alternative approach is presented for computing the mod $5$ counts of $5$-core partitions.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. We classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types - simple shifts, complex shifts, and distortions - and use a unique motion vector representation to safeguard against all possible movements, reaching remarkable robustness. With the introduction of phantom points, we also prevent injection of artificial points, significantly enhancing the robustness. Our framework has proven highly effective, with successful empirical evaluations on the MaskRCNNCar and SAMS point cloud models that surpass current standards for point cloud model security.

We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks with all radar units utilizing identical settings, such as sweep duration and frequency characteristics. We're developing and evaluating ALOHA and CSMA protocols to resolve transmission conflicts, with the CSMA method incorporating clear channel assessment, priority scheduling, and packet retransmission to manage packet collisions. Our performance analysis, gained from extensive simulation, indicates that the ALOHA and CSMA methods achieve comparable results to optimal theories, while the CSMA method outperforms ALOHA and exhibits similarities to slotted ALOHA.

Recent experiments employing various methods have sought to detect the entangled two-photon absorption phenomenon across a range of materials. A new approach is proposed to identify this phenomenon through a natural extension of the Michelson interferometer setup commonly used in entangled photon experiments. The proposed method is expected to offer a more direct indication of entangled two-photon absorption.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05, and the T^2-equivariant theory constructed in Bar22, share a key decomposition. This key decomposition facilitates reducing the T-equivariant cohomology computation to T^2-equivariant cohomology of complex spheres, whose computation is already available from Bar22.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to temporal constraints.
We recognize current limitations in temporal models, such as oversensitivity to
time, which can lead to suboptimal performance, and offer our time-parameterized
factorization model as a solution. Experimental results on multiple evaluation
datasets demonstrate time-lowFER's significant advancements over existing
state-of-the-art temporal factorization models, including improved KG embedding
accuracy and increased robustness to time parameters. The code for time-lowFER is
available at https://github.com/jbarchi/time-lowFER.

In the field of rigid-body impact sound synthesis, the sound produced by the ground is often overlooked. However, in this study, an idealized ground sound model, rooted in elastodynamic theory, is used to determine under which conditions ground sound is perceivable, rather than being masked by the sound produced by the impacting object or its transient vibrations. An analytical model derived from this theory allows for the calculation of the acceleration of the ground surface in a precise and mathematically closed form, which can then be applied in various simulation methods to generate the sound. It is found that ground sound can be audible under certain circumstances when the sound produced by the impacting object is inaudible, specifically when a heavy object strikes a soft surface and when the point of impact is positioned at a shallow angle relative to the listener's location.

A prevalent form of demonstrating Bell nonlocality known as the all-versus-nothing proof is presented without the use of inequalities. This concept consists of two main species, referred to as "always-type" and "sometimes-type", which have received significant research attention. Past studies on "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs have primarily involved perfect correlations from stabilizer states. This has led many to conclude that perfect correlations are the sole means of yielding "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs. Contrary to this prevailing notion, our study offers a "always-type" all-versus-nothing proof rooted in non-perfect correlations. This research aims to clarify an enduring misconception and potentially expands our understanding of Bell nonlocality while also opening avenues for advancements in quantum information technologies.

In flat band systems, constrained environments result in atypical behaviors influenced by randomness, indicating minimal movement. Molecular orbital representations of these systems introduce random MO models, retaining the degeneracy of the flat bands even in the presence of disorder. The success of this approach is evident in random tetrabenzoporphyrin lattices, exhibiting flat bands and associated Mo$\ddot{\text{u}}$ller-von Laue peaks. The properties of these systems can be captured by a simplified model of coupled rings with random hopping elements. The band structure of this model changes with the average hopping intensity, indicating various regimes including metallic and insulating states. The possibility of adjusting the orbital character involved in the flat bands by changing the coordination environment holds potential for optimizing the electronic properties of these systems.

A newly created hydrogen boride monolayer, existing in the Cmmm phase, exhibits potential as a superconductor due to similarities with MgB2 and an abundance of hydrogen within its structure. Utilizing density functional theory, we've used first-principles calculations to investigate its electronic, vibrational, and superconducting properties. Contrary to expectations, however, the hydrogen boride system displays an insulating state rather than a superconductor. Further analysis reveals that hydrostatic strain has a significant impact on the bonding between hydrogen and boron. Hydrogen, being highly compressible, forms a bond with boron that becomes increasingly covalent under strain, ultimately resulting in the formation of an insulating state. Notably, this phenomenon is observed in other hydrogen-containing materials such as NbH2 and that the bonding between hydrogen and boron can be altered through the use of external pressure.

Research on the division of quantities into equal parts continues to evolve. The findings presented here relate to the distribution of these parts into successive groups and the possible combinations of these groups, specifically the latter, which is referred to as the flattened version of the former. The underlying idea is represented by a specific type of sequence, where each term corresponds to a value in the division sequence divided by the smallest possible factor, then multiplied by the preceding term. This approach results in a sequence where each term exceeds the preceding one. It enables the identification of a particular subsequence, which reveals a connection to the representations of specific numbers as sums of squares. Moreover, using the eighth edition of the Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences, a particular sequence, denoted as A124324, is shown to be associated with this phenomenon; in addition, several additional relationships between terms of this sequence are presented, which pertain to both the representations of numbers as sums of squares and the cumulative sums of terms that are one more than the preceding term.

We categorize and understand a certain aspect of attractiveness in groups that use arithmetic, and derive statements indicating a dual nature related to their stable components, characteristics, patterns, and associated algebraic structures. To accomplish this, we study the movement patterns over the characteristics of the part of these groups that are stable and have manageable properties, particularly demonstrating the rigidity where any stable movement remains unchanged, which is a more comprehensive interpretation of Furstenberg's earlier work on almost-periodic patterns. Additionally, under the assumption that the group has a certain rigidity, we prove that the only stable characteristics are those that are well-known and have certain properties.

Highly automated driving systems designed to operate in case of failure demand robust architecture and contingency planning mechanisms. To effectively respond to failures, the system must leverage architecture-specific features, such as redundant components with divergent implementation, which can assume control in emergency situations. To ensure the effective response to failures, it is crucial to identify and capitalize on the advantages offered by the system's design. To this end, an innovative detection approach is introduced, capable of identifying failure recovery opportunities by analyzing the system's design description through model checking. The proposed method incorporates arithmetic expressions to represent the electrical connections between components and utilizes temporal logic to define desired recovery behaviors. It then employs model checking to identify scenarios where failure recovery is feasible and potentially fail-operational. The development of detection rules and the integration of arithmetic expressions require minimal expertise, thus providing flexible and adaptable solutions. Moreover, model checking ensures that detection rules are consistently applied, thereby mitigating the complexity of dynamic runtime evaluations. The introduction of a case study demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method in detecting failure recovery opportunities, showcasing its practical application and beneficial outcomes.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the application of spectral clustering to nonlinear dynamic systems. The approach is supported by extensive numerical experiments involving various synthetic and real-world cases.

Recent research into Leibnizian calculus has centered on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describe its mathematical processes.  Many scholars, such as Ishiguro and Levey, rely on a Weierstrassian perspective; in contrast, Arthur draws comparisons to the Lawvere-Kock-Bell framework, a non-Archimedean approach known as Smooth Infinitesimal Analysis (SIA). A critical examination of Arthur's comparison reveals significant misunderstandings regarding the nature of the continuous, polygons with an infinite number of sides, and infinitesimal quantities. Additionally, claims by Rabouin and Arthur, suggesting that Leibniz considered infinite quantities to be inherently contradictory, rely on an incorrect blending of Leibnizian concepts of bounded and unbounded infinites - a distinction previously noted by early Knobloch. Instead, a framework developed by Robinson may provide the most accurate account of Leibnizian calculus, which can be formalized using a conservative axiomatic system for infinitesimal analysis called SPOT. This formalisation covers concepts such as the bounded/unbounded distinction, a distinction between quantities that are or are not assigned to points, a generalised equality relation applicable to quantities differing by negligible terms, and a continuity principle.

Using the Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structure, we make predictions for HI intensity mapping power spectrum multipoles based on perturbation theory. These predictions will allow us to constrain cosmological parameters using mildly non-linear scales from data that will be obtained from interferometric HI intensity mapping experiments. Assuming that the experiments will be like CHORD and PUMA, we simulate the power spectrum multipoles for different redshift ranges and volume sizes. By comparing these simulations with the EFT predictions, we can determine the optimal redshift range and volume size for each model parameter. Based on this analysis, we derive new constraints for the cosmological parameters $A_s$, $\alpha$ and the neutrino mass $m_
u$. Specifically, we can determine $A_s$ with an accuracy of 5.1% and $m_
u$ with an accuracy of 0.6 eV when using a redshift range of 0.7 to 2. However, we find that the parameter $\alpha$ cannot be constrained from the HI intensity mapping power spectrum multipoles due to its degeneracy with the linear bias parameter. Furthermore, we find that a larger volume size increases the accuracy with which we can determine $m_
u$. Additionally, we find that a redshift range of 0.7 to 2 offers the optimal trade-off between the accuracy with which we can determine $m_
u$ and $A_s$.

Christensen and Hasannasab established that if a hypothetical operator T transforms sequence vectors $e_n$ into $e_{n+1}$ for all natural numbers, then the sequence is linearly independent only when the dimension of the sequence's vector space is infinite. In our research, we derive this result as a specific instance of a more comprehensive model-theoretic finding. Then, focusing on vector spaces, we demonstrate that if a condition such as $T(e_i)=e_{\phi(i)}$ is to replace the previous operator assumption, $\phi$ must be equivalent to the successor function, defined as incrementing a number by 1. Finally, we explore a more complex generalization of this result, substituting the earlier operator assumption with a more complex condition.

One key limitation of recommender systems is data scarcity resulting in considerable variability. Various approaches have been implemented to optimize the bias-variance equilibrium utilizing supplementary information. In particular, methods incorporating text-based document modeling have significantly improved accuracy by incorporating data like reviews, summaries, and narratives when user-item rating matrices are sparse. Nonetheless, these models are inadequate to learn optimal user and item representations. Collaborative filtering methods, including user-based and item-based, due to their efficiency and clarity, have long been utilized in building recommender systems by generating profiles for each user and item based on their historically interacted items and users. Our research integrates these methods with context-aware document models by taking into account users' perspectives on these items. Our novel context-aware CF model is an enhancement of traditional CF methods as it is compatible with various large-scale recommender systems. Our model's key advantage is its ability to learn user and item representation profiles. Our empirical evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate that our context-aware CF method outperforms traditional CF methods and document-based methods by a significant margin of up to 10%.

Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already known to result from this property. We've established an additional consequence: almost sure asymptotic freeness of type $B$ for unitarily invariant random matrices. This consequence leads to several secondary findings: the asymptotic cyclic monotonicity, and the derivation of asymptotic conditional freeness. Specifically, we demonstrate the empirical spectral distribution of randomly rotated matrices converges towards a conditionally free convolution. We've also identified new relationships between infinitesimal freeness, type $B$ freeness, conditional freeness, cyclic monotonicity, and monotone independence. Moreover, we show that the BBP phase transition in an additive rank-one perturbation of a GUE matrix is a consequence of asymptotic conditional freeness. This explanation supplements our previous understanding from random matrix perturbation theory.

This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties described as Metric Interval Temporal Logic formulas. Each formula consists of a predicate and a metric constraint, enabling adaptation of the Sistla, Copi, Maker model for efficient temporal logic monitoring under epsilon-distance under Abelian groups. We show that MITE under epsilon-distance on arbitrary sets is equivalent to a variant of Synchronous Products under a modified version of epsilon-distance on integer lattices. As a result, we derive a polynomial-time monitoring algorithm for any real-time system, provided that its model and dynamics are themselves polynomial-sized. In contrast to previous approaches for first-order logic and Michel's method for interval temporal logic, this method excels at handling both metric and traditional temporal logic formulas on real-time systems, including arbitrary, not just linear, architectures.

The decay reactions $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ and $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi
a_0(980)$ are examined in detail. Attention is focused on isospin breaking and
the mixing between $f_0(980)$ and $a_0(980)$, both of which are generated by meson-meson interactions. Our analysis indicates that the primary source of isospin breaking arises from transition matrix $T$ terms exhibiting isospin breaking and that additional isospin breaking arises due to the presence of loops containing kaons, as these do not cancel out when charged and neutral kaon masses differ. A calculated branching ratio for $a_0(980)$ production was found to be on the order of $5 \times 10^{-6}$.
