Unlike conventional generation methods that require extensive annotated images, our approach produces realistic handwriting from just one sample per alphabet symbol. After creating these symbols, synthetic lines are produced for training leading Handwritten Text Recognition models without the need for line segmentation. Thorough evaluation and analysis affirm the efficacy of the proposed solution.

We have developed a novel storage approach that significantly decreases the required memory by approximately two orders of magnitude, allowing us to compute three-nucleon interaction matrix elements with more precise limits in ab initio calculations. Our method, based on an approximate iterative method, is subsequently applied to calculate various properties related to the three-nucleon interaction. We utilize these computed matrix elements to investigate the properties of the deuteron and helium-4 nucleus. Our study on the deuteron focused on calculating its transition probabilities to various excited states, whereas we explored the energy spectra and decay widths of helium-4. Our calculated values are then compared with experimental data and theoretical predictions from other approaches. Our ab initio calculations, without any adjustments to the three-nucleon interaction, demonstrate good agreement with experimental data, indicating that the shell model description is sufficient to understand the properties of light nuclei and nuclear deexcitation.

We invite undergraduate students and early graduate students to an educational introduction to one-dimensional topological phases, focusing on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. This will include discussions on entanglement using the correlator method and von Neumann density matrix, as well as geometric phase, polarization, and transport characteristics, all with consideration of electron-electron interactions. Hands-on numerical experiments guided by publicly available codes are used to convey the value of using topological toy models for exploring new concepts in quantum electronics.

This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with certain bounded, convex domains in complex n-dimensional space containing non-trivial analytic circles in the boundary. Consequently, this characterizes compactness of the composition operator with a continuous symbol (limited to its closure) on the Bergman space of the polydisc.

We derived a formula for general single-spacelike, single-null gravitational amplitudes in AdS_4 space up to a null vector, employing a new set of integral transforms called zigzag integrals, which exhibit intriguing duality properties. By combining two distinct sets of zigzag integrals corresponding to spacelike and null directions, we obtained an explicit expression for the full gravitational amplitude. Our results can be represented either as a sum over gluon helicities or as a product of eigenvalues of specific AdS stress tensor components. Our findings also reveal a new connection between conformal operators in the boundary CFT, specifically for the cases of mixed and purely graviton amplitudes. By examining a specific subset of zigzag integrals, we were able to reproduce known AdS/CFT results for graviton amplitudes and provided new, more concise representations. Furthermore, we demonstrated how our general amplitude formula can be split into distinct components corresponding to gluing various AdS amplitudes involving fewer legs and massless components. By exploring a specific set of these'recursive zigzag integrals,' we obtained a new representation for the AdS quadrupole moment of a conformal operator, showcasing the role of Gubser stress, hydrodynamic coupling, and specific Casimir effect contributions.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with millions of lines of code, remain crucial for scientific research and offer significant performance improvement potential.  The problem of accessing memory on SIMD devices can be broken down into two distinct parts: memory allocation and data alignment.  The first issue, memory alignment, has been addressed by languages and compilers such as Fortran and C++ with various techniques.  However, the second issue, data alignment, remains largely unaddressed, resulting in suboptimal performance due to unnecessary memory copies, slow iterators, and unaligned memory access.  The data alignment problem is particularly pronounced in Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO) patterns, including vectorized loops, where a single method acts on multiple objects.  The consequence of neglecting data alignment is a substantial wasted potential, as demonstrated by our own analysis of which parts of real-world applications can be converted into SMMO patterns to achieve significant performance improvements.  The problem of data alignment has been addressed in vector languages such as Fortran, which provides a data alignment operator but is limited to array data type.  The question of how to effectively solve the data alignment problem for general object-oriented programming, including vectorized loops, has remained unresolved for many years.  In particular, compiler-based approaches have struggled to provide a practical solution

We introduce family universal U(1)X models incorporating three right-handed neutrinos, by defining U(1)X as a composite of SO(10) U(1)Y and U(1)χ gauge symmetries. To incorporate quantum gravity effects, the models are extended with the U(1)X gauge boson coupled to Ronald Wagoner's graviton, and thereby, the models become non-ultraviolet-finite models. However, we manage this infinity by confining it to neutrino masses through seesaw mechanisms involving the Wagoner's graviton. LHC constraints on Z' bosons are analyzed within the context of one-specific model of this class, consisting of mZ' ≈ 3 TeV mass Z' bosons. Our study reveals that model-based sensitivities on Z' couplings with Higgs bosons differ significantly from those based on top-quark processes. Furthermore, detection possibilities of dark matter, consisting of a sterile neutrino with approximately 1 eV mass, are explored in dark matter direct detection experiments within this class of models.

A specific measurement technique must be used for assessing the mechanical characteristics of straw tubes designed for charged particle detection, operating in a vacuum environment. The underlying equations that govern straw behavior when subjected to internal pressure are documented, alongside the introduction of an experimental approach in this paper to investigate strained, pressurized straw tubes. The presented research also focuses on measuring the Poisson's ratio of the straw wall for the NA62 spectrometer, with the ultimate goal of determining the minimum pre-tension required for the straw's structural stability.

In various fields, ensuring decision functions maintain their optimal performance under changing conditions, even with limited knowledge of their environment, is a top priority. Our study introduces an approach for quantifying how well decision functions withstand uncertainty in the form of credal Bayesian networks, which are parametric models representing the unknown environment with confidence intervals on key variables. Focusing on the 'Maximum Marginal Probability' (MARmax) issue – the maximum possible error probability when misclassifying data, given varying parameter possibilities – our approach transforms MARmax into a more manageable problem on a probabilistic circuit. Through a series of preprocessing steps involving circuit simplification and applying dual decomposition, we ultimately solve MARmax using a tractable optimization technique within a polytime framework. Our empirical evaluations show that the proposed solution quickly finds optimal marmax values, even with large circuit sizes.

In a supersolid Bose-Einstein condensate with a spin-orbit coupling, an accelerated impurity atom exhibits oscillations that mirror Bloch oscillations in solid matter, despite causing condensate excitements that give rise to internal phonon modes. However, these oscillations have no impact on the condensate's roton minimum position, thereby preserving its periodic matter wave pattern. Notably, the oscillations fade primarily due to wavepacket dispersal; yet, by assuming the impurity behaves as a bright soliton, the decay can be largely countered.

In a generalised quadrangle, a code is a subset of the vertices with its minimum distance determined by the shortest path between distinct elements. The elements of this subset are divided into distinct sets based on their distance from the code. Given the quadrangle's graph has a diameter of four, both the minimum distance and maximum distance from a vertex to its closest code element cannot exceed four. If the minimum distance is four, it signifies the code generates a subquadrangle through nearest neighbours; a code producing this subquadrangle for every element in the quadrangle is known as a thick code. A thick code exists within the quadracles of order three and quadrables of order five, with codes of order five possessing a minimum distance of two or four, and those of order three having a minimum distance of two. Researchers have discovered a code of order seven with a minimum distance of four, and through it, a thick code of order seven. This subquadrangle's existence contradicts a conjecture by Van Malta and Camion, suggesting no thick code of order seven exists.

Located at the heart of the Milky Way's Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), lies a massive molecular complex, referred to as the Filsia molecular complex (FMC). This important complex, labeled as a complex in the CMZ, has been recognized for its distinct ring-like shape and significant mass content. Given its location near the CMZ's center, it has been proposed that the FMC drives the expansion of the zone. To assess this theory, scientists have examined the evidence for a mass flux from the FMC. By utilizing data from radio observations, they found that the FMC contains a central void area and two spiral arms composed of molecular gas. Additionally, it has been proposed that a mass flux may be directed towards a large void area in the CMZ, known as the Hoover void. This theory is based on the observation of a mass distribution gradient across this area. By further investigating the mass distribution and motion within and around the FMC, scientists have found evidence for two distinct gas components in the area. This research suggests that the FMC and the Hoover void are separate entities and a mass flux from the FMC to the CMZ has yet to be confirmed. By further examining the mass distribution and motion within the CMZ, scientists have found clues indicating the presence of a massive black hole at the area's center. This discovery has further increased speculation that the CMZ and the surrounding areas may eventually form a supermassive star-forming region, known as a globular

Subjecting solid materials to an ultra-intense, femtosecond X-ray pulse from a free-electron laser causes drastic electronic excitation, triggering swift changes within the material's electronic system that unfold over the duration of the pulse. The amount of X-rays absorbed by the material becomes contingent upon the energy flux, giving rise to a unique form of X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy. Researchers can study valence excitation on the few-femtosecond timescale with this type of XANES spectroscopy, allowing for in-depth examination of electronic dynamics close to the Fermi level.

To develop an comprehensive framework for understanding the insulator-to-metal transition induced by femtosecond laser pulses, we combined experimental results with detailed theoretical models. Our research centered on nitrogen gas, focusing on the interplay between multicenter ionization and single-photon ionization. The creation of a nitrogen plasma by a pulse with low energy density results in an insulating state, characterized by a cutoff in electron absorption at a certain energy level. As the plasma becomes more electron-dense due to increased pulse intensity, the cutoff shifts to higher energy levels and conductivity begins. Longer interaction times lead to a situation where the plasma's mean free path for scattering equals the interatomic distance, resulting in a shift in the absorption edge to higher energy levels in this regime. Our experiments confirmed these predictions, offering a comprehensive understanding of electron dynamics within a metal-insulator transition. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert thermal data into two distinguishable current ratios, which are then analyzed by a binary classifier to estimate the temperature. The proposed design offers high accuracy, minimal current consumption, and efficient disturbance rejection, while also facilitating integration with existing adaptive voltage and frequency scaling systems. The implementation details are validated through experimental results obtained from a 28nm CMOS process, demonstrating a less than 0.25 % absolute error for all possible temperature readings.

Quantum entanglement serves as a cornerstone for quantum information science and technologies. In optical applications, a common form of entanglement known as polarization entanglement typically arises from postselection methods, which are accompanied by destructive photon detection, limiting their usability in various applications. In this research, a new strategy is proposed to create entangled states of polarized photons without requiring postselection, instead opting for a heralded approach that ensures ready availability of entangled resources. By applying the quantum scissors technique to manipulate a specific type of entanglement known as continuous-variable entanglement, it is possible to create the desired entangled states without compromising on quality. We present two practical methods for achieving polarization entanglement using the quantum scissors technique, both based on cavityless parametric down conversion sources. The first method involves manipulating a source with two input modes producing entanglement in a specific variable known as squeezing, while the second method involves manipulating a source with three input modes producing entanglement in a specific variable known as mode convention. The research demonstrates that the quantum scissors technique can create polarization entangled states in a heralded manner, paving the way for its use in free-space quantum key distribution applications.

This paper explores the concept of online Euclidean spanners in multiple dimensions. It considers the case where a sequence of points in R^d is given one at a time, and an algorithm must create and update a geometric t-spanner for each set of points as it arrives. Initially, the authors establish a lower bound of at least 1 + 1/n for the competitive ratio of any online 1+1-spanner algorithm in one dimension, demonstrating that a particular random sequence of points in R^2 can lead to suboptimal performance for any such algorithm. Building on this finding, the authors present improved online 2-spanner algorithms for R^d, narrowing the gap between known upper and lower bounds in the case of points in R^2. The authors also examine the possibility of designing algorithmically simple online Euclidean spanners and present evidence suggesting that any such algorithm for points in R^2 would have a competitive ratio of at most 5/3.

Accurate categorization of IoT devices is a vital requirement, with implications extending to security and data protection aspects. Research has successfully applied machine learning methods for identifying IoT devices, with positive outcomes. However, these studies overlooked a crucial factor - the cost of extracting features from devices. This research investigates whether feature extraction costs vary significantly across different IoT devices, with implications for classification. Building on existing work, we compiled a dataset with 122 devices from six categories, using three feature extraction methods with distinct costs. Our analysis reveals that, although some devices are easily identifiable with less expensive features, others require more expensive features for accurate classification. Notably, this research discovers a 'gray area' where some devices can be mistakenly classified as multiple categories using less expensive features. With growing security threats against IoT devices, knowing the feature extraction cost becomes essential for defending against malicious activities, with potential consequences being financial loss or compromised device security. This research sets the groundwork for exploring feature extraction costs in IoT device classification.

Godel modal logics can be regarded as an extension of intutionistic modal logics with prelinearity. In this study, we examine algebraic and relational semantics for Godel modal logics with unrestricted intersection. The underlying algebraic structure is the dSAlgebra, an extension of BL-algebras with dS-operations, and the relational semantics is the dS-atoms framework. Both the algebraic and relational approaches satisfy the properties of distributivity, associativity, and unidistributivity. The introduction of the dS-atoms framework allows for a general exploration of algebraic structures through specific examples such as modal Heyting algebras with prelinearity and positive classical modal logic with prelinearity.

This research presents a novel and straightforward technique for word-alignment that leverages bilingual information from external sources like machine translation platforms. We demonstrate that a model with limited parameters can achieve performance comparable to GIZA++ when trained on a relatively small dataset. Furthermore, in terms of alignment metrics, such as accuracy or F-score, our approach delivers results equivalent to GIZA++ when trained on a dataset 22 times smaller. Crucially, the method's domain-agnostic training capabilities enable 'on-the-fly' application on any new pair of sentences without requiring extensive retraining.

We suggest an asynchronous algorithm to solve Nash equilibrium problems by iteratively decomposing the mixed strategies. This methodology translates various Nash equilibrium challenges into a series of convex optimization tasks that can be resolved using established methods. Although we introduce a new Asynchronous Nash Equilibrium Algorithm, our primary contribution lies in proving its global convergence to the optimal solution. This asymptotic convergence is confirmed through an accessible and easy-to-understand proof. Additionally, we demonstrate that our algorithm exhibits faster execution time compared to its synchronous counterpart. Furthermore, we successfully apply the Asynchronous Nash Equilibrium Algorithm to resolve a stackelberg game and a Bertrand duopoly competition.

The theoretical primordial black holes that may have formed in the early universe are proposed as a possible type of dark matter. If these black holes exist, they can potentially be identified through specific star-related signals resulting from gravitational lensing. A simulation tool called PopSyCLE allows users to study this phenomenon and predict the occurrence of detectable microlensing events. To assess the likelihood of PBHs representing 100% of dark matter, we analyzed the predicted microlensing rates and observability of these events, utilizing the PopSyCLE simulator in conjunction with an advanced light cone simulation technique. Our simulations based on PBHs comprising all dark matter reveal that about 40% of PBHs are predicted to be embedded within the observable universe. However, our detailed light cone simulations showed that the predicted microlensing rate is significantly lower than previous estimates obtained through population synthesis methods. As a result, the predicted number of microlensing events per year per solar mass is much lower than the actual number of microlensing events per year per solar mass measured by the current Microlensing Telescope Network. Based on these simulations, we conclude it is highly unlikely that PBHs constitute 100% of dark matter. If PBHs exist, they likely make up a tiny fraction of the total dark matter.

We conducted research into systems at equilibrium consisting of uniform wedge-shaped molecules using Monte Carlo simulations, where each molecule consisted of six aligned spheres of gradually decreasing sizes, and the shape of these molecules was defined solely by the ratio of the smallest to the largest sphere diameters, referred to as parameter $d$. The systems' phases were studied as a function of parameter $d$ and the packing density of molecules $\eta$, under the condition that only repulsive interactions were present. This led to the system's behavior being controlled solely by the entropy of molecular arrangement. For systems where parameter $d$ varied and the packing density was low, less dense layers of molecules formed and the system displayed nematic and smectic A liquid crystalline phases. Conversely, when parameter $d$ was fixed but the packing density was low, the system displayed all nematic, herringbone and antiparallel layers of molecules. Furthermore, when the width of parameter $d$ was significant, the system displayed multiple layer packings of molecules with varying layer density and displayed multiple liquid crystalline phases that were not dependent on parameter $d$. When parameter $d$ was narrow, the system displayed low density of molecules with nematic and hexagonal monocrystalline phases, while also displaying multiple reentrant behavior for smectic and nematic phases.

Recurrences in the parameters of special functions often involve shifting indices in one parameter while keeping others constant. This paper expands upon a broader class of such recurrences that incorporate special functions with multiple parameters. Initially, we will derive an expression that relates the $n$th Gegenbauer polynomials with shifted Gegenbauer parameters $\kappa$ and $\lambda$. This relationship holds for all values of $n$, $\kappa$ and $\lambda$. Subsequently, we will establish the connection between Zonal Spherical Harmonics (ZSHs) and Gegenbauer polynomials, thereby deriving relationships between ZSHs with shifted parameters. Finally, we will use these relationships to prove the positive definiteness of a zonal function on the sphere, thereby answering a long-standing question. Our proof relies on the uniqueness of an important polynomial, thereby demonstrating its utility in various mathematical fields such as special functions, spherical functions and positive definite functions.

A conventional imaging scenario hinges on three essential elements: a light source that illuminates and scatters off the subject of interest; a means to detect this scattered light; and a detector that can resolve spatial information. However, the typical ingredients of imaging may be insufficient for biological specimens or other delicate objects due to the damage that light can cause, thereby necessitating alternative detection methods. One such alternative is to use quantum entanglement to retrieve information about a object's structure. In this study, we demonstrate that it is possible to collect detailed information about an object's internal structure using only one of the ingredients of imaging, specifically by utilizing the object's impact on the quantum entanglement of two detectors. This process is exemplified in a scenario where we obtain a object's internal structure using only scattered light and no need for a light source or a detector. Furthermore, we illustrate that it is feasible to obtain information about a object's structure even when the object is not interacting with any light, by utilizing quantum entanglement and reflecting light off a nearby reference object. This research expands our understanding of what it means to take an image of an object and may lead to the development of new and non-destructive imaging techniques.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated by comparing them with theoretical predictions for the "stationary" regime. The observation of non-dissipative stress in the "slip" regime challenges the current understanding of stress in complex liquids, while the "stick-slip" regime itself remains largely unexplained.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective.

We carried out a high-resolution ARPES study on sodium and found that the observed enhancement of its electronic mass is slightly less than expected from earlier research. These findings amplify the need for theoretical models more advanced than the random phase approximation. Contrary to the hypothesis suggesting significant acceleration of the carriers due to their interaction with spin fluctuations, our results do not support this theory. Additionally, a comparison with previous electron loss data indicates that sodium's mass enhancement due to dipole-type electron-hole interactions is substantially less than its mass enhancement due to monopole-type interactions measured using ARPES.

Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've successfully applied it to examine the dynamics of systems undergoing expansion or contraction, despite a significant challenge. Traditional methods in thermodynamics break down for such scenarios due to the issue of defining a signally variable that governs heat transfer. We've tackled this problem by analyzing the expansion of an ideal gas in a sealed environment and finding that the sign of the work done by the gas remains positive throughout the process. Our analysis provides a consistent framework for understanding the thermodynamics of systems that change size.

This passage provides an in-depth, explicit calculation for the weights of Kontsevich graphs that emerge from connections and curvatures within a symplectic manifold framework, specifically focusing on globalization. We'll demonstrate how curvature graph weights can be explicitly defined through a hypergeometric function and an even simpler expression that combines it with a formula for the underlying connection graph weights. Notably, we examine a cotangent bundle case, leading to a substantial simplification of the curvature expression.

We explore solitary waves known as "nanoptera," characterized by exponentially small oscillations, in two precompressed systems based on the Hertzian model, particularly woodpile chains and diatomic chains with alternating masses. These solitary waves emerge from the Stokes phenomenon as special curves in the complex plane are intersected, producing exponential asymptotics approximations. Our analysis reveals that solitary waves in precompressed woodpile chains feature a single Stokes curve, accompanied by oscillations, whereas a diatomic chain exhibits two Stokes curves, resulting in oscillations with opposite signs, thus potentially eliminating nanoptera.

Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can generate massive particles exceeding the Hubble scale during inflation. This prospect expands the scope of cosmological collider physics, where the signals produced by these particles are usually suppressed by the Boltzmann distribution. Our analysis explores the mechanics of a cosmic collider through two types of primordial features. Firstly, we consider oscillating primordial features, encompassing cases of massive field oscillations and oscillatory features in the inflationary potential. Secondly, we look at any sharp feature within an inflationary model. These features can induce unsuppressed quantum fluctuations in heavy fields, leaving detectable signatures in primordial non-Gaussian patterns, and revealing details about the spectra of these heavy degrees of freedom.

Consider a graph of even order G and its complete graph counterpart K_G. A pairing of G refers to a perfect matching of K_G. A graph has the PH-property if for each pairing of K_G, it shares a perfect matching that, when combined, creates a Hamiltonian cycle of K_G. Cubic graphs that possess the PH-property have been fully characterized by Alahmadi et al. in 2015, and it follows logically that quartic graphs should be the subject of characterization next. In our work, a class of quartic graphs called accordion graphs is defined, parameterized by n and k, which we designate as A[n,k]. We find that a specified family of infinite quartic (also circulant) graphs that possess the PH-property belong to the general class of accordion graphs. The paper delves into the properties of accordion graphs in terms of their existence, which is easily understood, which which which which which existence which which which which which which which which which which which which which which which which which which which which which which existence. A plethora of infinite classes of quartic graphs which possess the PH-property are easily seen to be contained within the accordion graph class for which we provide a generic representation. which which which which which which which which which which which which which which which which which which which which which which which which which which which.

We carry out a finite-time scaling analysis near the detrapping point in a three-state quantum walk model. The coin operator is adjusted using parameter $\rho$ that controls the speed of wavepacket dispersion. The initial state is a symmetric superposition of two coin operator eigenstates with mixing angle $\theta$. One eigenstate corresponds to full wavepacket spreading at $\theta_c(\rho)$ where none of the wavepacket remains near the initial position. At the detrapping angle, key metrics such as survival probability and participation ratio exhibit one-parameter scaling behavior. Moreover, we demonstrate that the participation ratio grows with time, specifically in a logarithmic-corrected linear fashion, thereby resolving reported sublinear tendencies.

This paper investigates the benefits of self-supervised learning for semantic segmentation. Unlike traditional convolutional networks, which often rely on labeled data, self-supervised learning allows models to be pre-trained without prior annotation. We demonstrate that a self-supervised Vision Transformer can achieve superior results compared to its supervised counterpart and convolutional network equivalents, performance that remains consistent even when labeled data becomes available. This unique finding suggests that pre-trained self-supervised models like our DRL-BN-CAE can serve as highly effective feature extractors, yielding exceptional results whether used as a feature for a linear classifier or a feature for end-to-end training in a segmentation task.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics and identify regions that could potentially be characterized as phantom or standard. Furthermore, through numerical calculations of the Hubble parameter and deceleration parameter, we found that this model aligns with the accelerated cosmological model's observational data.

We present a straightforward proof that in three or more dimensions, the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations has a critical issue in terms of stability, specifically when using Sobolev spaces and certain types of Lorentz spaces, thereby confirming an earlier study by Bourgain and Li.

Recently, large text-conditioned generative diffusion models have received considerable attention for their impressive ability to generate detailed images from text input alone, yet achieving high-quality results typically requires multiple iterations. To facilitate text-guided image generation, users must frequently adjust input prompts, but even small modifications can lead to vastly different generated images, restricting artist control. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Stable Artist, an image editing technique allowing artists to exert precise control over the image generation process. Its key component is semantic guidance (SEGA), enabling the diffusion process to be directed by multiple, varying semantic axes, thereby permitting refined edits to images and prompts. When applied to artists' sketches, the Stable Artist produces unparalleled generation quality after just one text input, as evidenced by the extraordinary 4x performance gain over existing methods. Moreover, SEGA facilitates diverse generative tasks like discrete text-to-image generation and artist-directed image transformation, resulting in the most realistic and varied outcomes from any text or sketch input.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. Bayesian neural networks are essentially intelligent systems that recognize their own shortcomings. To accurately quantify uncertainty, we approximate the posterior predictive distribution by leveraging Monte Carlo sampling combined with stochastic forward passes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that predictive uncertainty can be separated into aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, both of which can be learned in the form of deterministic neural networks. A series of empirical tests confirm that the proposed method effectively quantifies uncertainty and leads to improved steganographic encoding and decoding processes.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a model of sub-GeV dark matter based on a fermion with a lepton-like doublet. Our analysis focuses on final states containing electrons or muons along with large amounts of invisible matter that could be neutrinos, dark matter particles, or gauge bosons such as the Z prime. A thorough review of past J/ψ experiments, particularly those conducted by Belle and BABAR, reveals that they already set significant limits on general neutrino interactions and provide new, tightened restrictions on the parameter spaces for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. Our research also discovers that J/ψ decay into invisible matter may be a more sensitive method of detecting dark matter than other processes, such as dark matter absorption within atomic hydrogen.

High-resolution observations of the solar photosphere reveal tiny magnetic bright points, associated with extremely strong magnetic fields, present throughout the solar cycle. These features, extensively detected in solar images, play a significant role in understanding the solar atmosphere's behavior, particularly in addressing the long-standing question of coronal heating. This research aimed to examine the size, speed, and distribution patterns of magnetic bright points in the solar photosphere, using the SOT/Hinode instrument at 0.66 micron, to gain insights into their characteristics. Results from both polar regions, obtained during a period of low solar activity, show magnetic bright points are concentrated, with their speeds and distributions matched by a Boltzmann distribution. These findings indicate the presence of two distinct populations of magnetic bright points, consisting of smaller and faster ones associated with faster and larger ones moving slower. The length and energy distributions of magnetic bright points, however, require a more complex explanation, suggesting the possibility of two distinct populations, as well.

Human vision can distinguish objects and actions using spatial or temporal data, but integrating these aspects remains unclear. This study demonstrates how the human visual system can effectively combine spatial and motion information, enabling recognition in scenarios where individual sources are insufficient. Researchers achieved this insight by analyzing'minimal videos' - brief clips that facilitate reliable object, part, and action recognition, but are unrecognizable when spatial or temporal constraints are compromised. Unlike existing deep networks, humans exhibit more adept performance in these complex configurations, highlighting missing dynamic vision mechanisms in current models.

Dark particles interacting through Abelian gauge symmetries and ordinary matter through kinetic mixing result in the manifestation of broken $U(1)$ magnetic monopoles in our observable universe as milli-magnetically charged entities called "dark magnetic monopoles." Although the existence of electrically charged entities has been ruled out by experiments, the possibility of the existence of milli-magnetically charged entities called "dark magnetic monopoles" cannot be dismissed. If such entities exist, they would likely be found in the galactic halo. As these entities move, they cause an anisotropic scattering of cosmic microwave background photons, leading to a suppression of the $E/B$ mode ratio. This, in turn, allows for a constraint to be placed on the ellipticity of the halo monopoles can be constrained by the BICEP2/POLARBEAR data, effectively ruling out monopoles with ellipticity greater than 0.25, although ellipticity less than 0.25 remains a possibility. Upcoming data from Planck and CMB-S4 are expected to further tighten these constraints, potentially setting an ellipticity limit at 0.25 or tighter.

The rapidly evolving Earth Observatory research area has immense potential to utilize AI in real-time weather forecasting. This work addresses the challenge of accurate weather prediction by leveraging the video transformer network. Building on existing research into vision transformer architectures, we address the limitations associated with their high computational complexity and data-hungry nature. To achieve this, we propose combining Video Swin-Transformer with a dedicated data augmentation method, and employing a gradual spatial reduction on the encoder and cross-attention on the decoder. The efficacy of our proposed approach was tested on the Weather4Cast2021 challenge dataset, where we successfully predicted 8 hours of future weather frames from hourly weather sequences. After normalizing the dataset for evaluation consistency, our model achieved an MSE score of 0.4750 using training data, and 0.4420 using transfer learning without training data.

In models that expand on the electroweak sector, a basis can be found where the symmetry prevents coupling, leading to viable dark matter candidates. Specifically, we analyze the $S_3$-symmetric three-Higgs-doublet models that allow softly broken $S_3$ terms, determining which models can host dark matter. The variety of models arises from different arrangements of vacuum expectation values, leading to vacua with either one or two vanishing expectation values. In our research, we focus on models featuring two non-vanishing doublets with a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry separating the two, enabling a dark matter candidate from a single doublet. Our findings indicate that some of these models are compatible with a dark matter candidate and also with the Higgs boson properties and electroweak and vacuum stability. We verified that the $S_3$-symmetric three-Higgs-doublet models produce viable dark matter candidates and are compatible with current data.

A comprehensive study on the PPT square conjecture is presented with a notable achievement: the PPT square conjecture's validity has been rigorously demonstrated for the case involving finite-dimensional space.

Intracellular transportation is crucial for delivering vital substances to complex branched neural structures, enabling their survival and operation. Disruption of this process is associated with various neurodegenerative diseases, making it vital to understand how neurons control transportation to target essential areas. We introduce a new optimization model that simulates the material transportation mechanism in complex neural geometries by minimizing congestion. The model adheres to partial differential equations that describe transportation based on molecular-motor-assisted models, and we propose a novel objective function that quantifies congestion through flow obstructions. To solve this complex problem, we utilize a code reformulation technique and an iterative algorithm combining the optimal transport bregman iterative method with the active set method, utility function method, and level-set morphing. We tested and validated our approach by successfully solving various numerical examples and simulating how material flows through complex neural structures with optimal traffic, as evidenced by our results.

Billion-dollar losses inflicted by banking fraud across the globe make it a pressing issue. To effectively detect fraud, it is crucial to understand the underlying patterns. Real-world transactions exhibit structural characteristics that can be analyzed using graph theory. In this study, we examine the prevalence of specific patterns, known as network motifs, within fraud-free and fraudulent transaction graphs. Our findings reveal an imbalance in the occurrence of these patterns, which can serve as a fraud indicator. Additionally, we stack different features, including the likelihood of specific patterns, to enhance the accuracy of fraud detection. Our results demonstrate that using a simplified version of these features can surpass the performance of sophisticated, complex methods on real-world datasets.

In a black hole-white dwarf binary system, we examine electromagnetic and gravitational waves emitted during a process where a white dwarf loses mass to a black hole through tidal forces. We simulate this scenario using a quantum hydrodynamic model and represent the white dwarf as a zero-temperature Bose-Fermi droplet. When the white dwarf approaches its point of closest approach to the black hole, it loses a small, high-density patch of material. This lost material emits intense bursts of gravitational waves, electrons, positrons, and gamma rays. The energy released from these bursts could potentially exceed $10^{49}$ erg. The frequency of these bursts, determined by the mass of the white dwarf and its size, can vary significantly and potentially be identified by LISA. The intense radiation could also potentially be detected by the Gamma-Ray Observatory. We anticipate that similar tidal interactions may occur in neutron star-white dwarf binaries and possibly in other binary systems containing compact objects.

Three-body $\tau$-decays, which involve semileptonic interactions with light hadrons and CP symmetry violations, can provide insight into these processes. Studies of weak electromagnetic interactions rely on form factors to describe the hadronic part of the final states, which can be further understood by decomposing the hadronic current into specific orbital angular momentum components. Given the increasing data availability from future $\tau$-decays and potential new lattice QCD simulations, researching three-body $\tau$-decays becomes particularly relevant. The article discusses current knowledge of the form factors involved and the significance of further research in this field.

Jim\'enez, Becerra, and Gelbukh (2013) introduced the "symmetric Tversky ratio models" with parameters $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ where $\alpha$ ranges between $0$ and $1$ and $\beta$ is greater than $0$. The inverse of each $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ function, denoted as $D_{\alpha,\beta}$, represents a semimetric for all possible subsets of a given set. Our research found that the function $D_{\alpha,\beta}$ is indeed a metric if $\alpha$ lies within the interval from $0$ to $0.5$ and $\beta$ is greater than or equal to $1/(1-\alpha)$. The verification of this outcome was successfully demonstrated in the Lean proof assistant. This parametrized space contains extreme points including $J_1 = D_{1/2,2}$, known as the Jaccard distance, and $J_{\infty} = D_{0,1}$, an analogue of the Li-Ma-Vit\'anyi information distance (2004) that has been normalized.

Modern motion deblurring methods based on deep learning utilize paired synthetic data for training frameworks, aiming to directly convert blurry inputs to clear outputs. However, the success of these methods heavily relies on high-quality synthetic blurry data, which is both time-consuming and expensive to generate. To make matters worse, real-world blurry data often cannot be directly paired with clear images due to the complexity of deblurring processes, particularly in cases with severe motion and low-resolution scenarios. To overcome these challenges, we introduce an innovative method called Self-Deblurring Network (SDNet), which seamlessly integrates self-supervised learning with conventional supervisory signals. By doing so, SDNet enables the effective use of unpaired data for motion deblurring, significantly expanding the scope of this technique. Moreover, our model is the first to apply an unsupervised blur variance estimation, thereby simplifying data generation processes, especially with video data. Experimental results demonstrate that SDNet outperforms the current state-of-the-art motion deblurring models by achieving noticeable improvements in unsupervised and weakly supervised settings, particularly with object-based supervision, which poses a more complex challenge.

Hebbian theory aims to explain how brain cells modify their responses to stimuli, ultimately leading to the ability to learn. A notable aspect of Hebbian learning is its ability to occur independently, without requiring external feedback. This concept has been embodied in spiking neural networks through the introduction of homeostatic plasticity mechanisms. These theories, however, often rely on unsupervised learning paradigms with predefined network structures, limiting their applicability to more complex systems. This research presents an alternative approach to independent learning, focusing on a more flexible pre-synaptic configuration. It shows that pre-synaptic neurons with adjustable connections can develop optimal wiring configurations, allowing them to solve complex problems such as clustering and separating data, all without any external influence or prior knowledge of the network structure. Furthermore, it is observed that the resulting connections within the pre-synaptic system exhibit a high degree of organization, resembling that found in biological synapses. Finally, it is demonstrated that the obtained flexible configurations can be applied to a variety of challenging tasks in machine learning, including classification tasks, where external feedback is unavailable or incomplete.

The ultrapower of any ordered set is created as a refined version of the set itself by taking into account infinite sequences of elements from it. This process involves dividing the sequences into classes according to a set of rules defined by an ultrafilter, leading to a set that always satisfies a fundamental property of ordered sets. It turns out that a set's openness determines its ability to fulfill the open completeness property in the refined version, whereas its original cardinality dictates whether the refined version is complete.

Scientific breakthroughs in data-driven science increasingly rely on applying sophisticated AI models to comprehensive, discipline-specific datasets. However, the computational intelligence of traditional machine learning methods can sometimes lead them off track, resulting in lower accuracy. This research investigates how to select the best computational method for a given problem and dataset, by utilizing a comprehensive dataset index and comparison tool. The index, developed under a National Science Foundation grant, is being expanded to include more scientific domains and their associated datasets, benchmarks, methods, and research papers. Preliminary study results demonstrate that model ranking varies significantly across different scientific datasets and domains, highlighting the need for tailored index development. Additionally, an online platform and mobile app enable active learning dataset indexing and real-time model ranking access.

Hadwiger's Coloring Conjecture asserts that every graph with t colors includes a complete graph with t vertices. This has been reinforced by another theory suggesting if a given graph is assigned t colors, where a certain set of its vertices uses every possible color, then that graph must have a complete graph with t vertices within it. This more robust idea has been tested with success for the case of t = 4. This result holds further implications for 5-colored graphs; specifically, we can confirm a revised and more robust version of the original Hadwiger's conjecture, where 5-colored graphs contain complete graphs with 5 vertices within them. This has further implications for 5-critical graphs in the same scenario.

This paper introduces an advanced algorithm for efficiently recovering smooth graph signals through generalized correntropy, and a specific loss function is formulated accordingly. The algorithm is sophisticated and adaptive, and the efficacy of its predictions depends on the kernel's width parameter, which needs to be optimized. To overcome this challenge, the paper derives a optimal kernel width by analyzing the worst-case prediction error, and the resulting loss function is examined in relation to the traditional least-squares method. Additionally, the paper develops an iterative optimization procedure for efficient kernel-based signal recovery. The efficacy of the proposed algorithm is validated through numerical experiments conducted on diverse networks, and the results indicate that it excels at various smoothing levels.

Theoretical investigations are conducted to design and control entangled atomic states formed through spin-changing collisions within a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate for use in a more robust atom interferometry capable of withstanding common technical problems like detector limitations. It is discovered through both analytical and numerical examinations of the spin-changing collision process that utilizing a small initial disturbance as a trigger, as opposed to vacuum fluctuations, yields superior results despite reduced entanglement. Our findings have implications for optimizing entangled atomic state production for quantum-enhanced matter-wave interferometry applications.

The paper explores the optimal first eigenvalue for the anisotropic $p$-Laplace operator subject to a non-local boundary condition derived from the first Robin eigenvalue on a bounded $C^{1}$-domain. This eigenvalue problem is influenced by the orientation and size of the domain as well as its normal vector. As key factors arise from the condition that the 'weight' function has a strong relationship with the domain's boundary, particularly when it occurs with a sign change, we establish precise estimates of this eigenvalue in terms of $p$. Additionally, we analyze its asymptotic behavior as $p$ approaches 1 or becomes large. Moreover, we investigate its behavior under various domain transformations, specifically how it changes with a linear scaling factor in one dimension, a dilatation in two or three dimensions, and how it undergoes a transformation via a diffeomorphism in any number of dimensions.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of irregularly-sampled data through the adoption of a continuous-time learning framework known as GCNNs and associated kernel networks, which are rebranded as Continuous Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (CGCNNs). The CGCNN formulation facilitates the creation of specialized sensors by optimizing the design of the matching kernel. Additionally, a novel Stochastic Graph Convolutional Neural Network (SGCNN) is developed by combining the CGCNN formulation with a Bayesian learning paradigm, enabling the CGCNN to learn from data with irregularly spaced samples. The efficacy of these new methods is substantiated in simulation experiments involving irregularly-sampled time-series data, showing improved performance over traditional GCNNs and competing methods.

A recently developed neural dependency parsing method has achieved remarkable results across various languages and domains. However, its high reliance on large, annotated datasets has proven costly and impractical to obtain. This paper proposes a novel self-training technique that mitigates this data annotation constraint by leveraging the parser's own output to improve performance. Specifically, the Deep Contextualized Self-training algorithm integrates external sequence models, derived from the parser's application to unlabelled data, into the parser using a sophisticated weighting system. Comprehensive experiments have been conducted across multiple languages in diverse settings, and the results clearly indicate that our approach outperforms traditional self-training and state-of-the-art semi-supervised learning methods by a significant margin.

We've investigated the transition form factors $f_+(q^2)$ and $f_-(q^2)$ [alternatively $f_0(q^2)$] for exclusive semileptonic $B	o D\ell
u_\ell$ $(\ell=e,\mu,	au)$ decays using the standard light-front quark model based on light-front quantization. Conventionally, $f_+(q^2)$ can be determined without considering troublesome elements, but $f_-(q^2)$ typically includes such difficulties. However, our study reveals in the Drell-Yan frame ($q^+=0$) that the results obtained using $(J^+, J^-)$ for $f_-(q^2)$ are equivalent to those derived from $(J^+, { f J}_\perp)$ without including treacherous components. Furthermore, our calculations provided the form factors and branching ratios for $B	o D\ell
